Lǔ Táo Yīng (魯陶嬰) was the daughter of Táo Míng (陶明).
She was widowed young,
raising a young orphan without strong brothers,
spinning and weaving for a living.
Some people in Lǔ (魯) heard of her righteousness
and wanted to seek her [in marriage].
Yīng (嬰) heard of this
and, fearing she could not avoid it,
composed the Song of the Yellow Swan,
making clear her resolve not to remarry.
They understood that he would not change his mind after two trials,
the people of Lu heard of it,
and therefore dared not seek (a judgement) again.
Superior
He stopped
Wáng Zhāng, styled Zhòngqīng,
lived alone with his wife,
sick, without a blanket, lying in a cattle coat,
bidding farewell to his wife in tears,
his wife scolded him angrily, saying:
"Zhòngqīng is honorable,
in the court, who surpasses Zhòngqīng?
Now, sick and distressed,
you do not encourage yourself,
but instead weep, how base!"
Later, Zhāng served as the governor of Jīngzhào,
wanting to submit a memorial speaking of the emperor's uncle Wáng Fèng,
his wife stopped him, saying:
"People should know contentment,
do you not remember the weeping in the cattle coat?"
Zhāng said:
"It is not something a woman can understand."
The memorial was then submitted,
and as a result, he was imprisoned by the court and died.
《Book of Han》
Revenge
Guī Lǎn and Dài Yuán, being close to Biān Hóng and others, were often troubled by Sūn Yì,
and constantly desired to rebel.
At that time, the magistrates of the various counties all came to see Yì.
Yì, knowing that his wife, Xú Shì, was somewhat skilled in divination,
Yì entered and said to Xú:
"Tomorrow, I intend to play host to the magistrates,
why don't you try to divine the outcome?"
Xú said:
"The divination is not auspicious,
it would be better to postpone it to another day."
Yì thought that the magistrates had been asking for a long time and should be sent away quickly,
so he held a large banquet for the guests.
Yì went out to see off the guests,
Hóng then assassinated him from behind,
and fled in revolt into the mountains.
Xú Shì offered rewards to hunt him down.
Lǎn and Yuán blamed and killed Hóng.
The generals all knew that Lǎn and Yuán were responsible but lacked the power to punish them.
Lǎn entered and resided in the military headquarters,
taking all of Yì's concubines and attendants.
He also wanted to take Xú,
fearing that she might be harmed if she resisted.
Therefore, he deceived her, saying:
"I ask to wait until the last day of the month for the sacrificial ceremony to remove the mourning clothes, as the month is almost over."
Lǎn agreed to wait until the sacrifice was completed.
Xú secretly sent her trusted confidants to convey her intentions to Sūn Gāo, Fù Yīng, and other old generals who were close to Yì.
Gāo and Yīng wept and complied.
Then, they secretly summoned more than twenty attendants who had served Yì,
They together swore an oath and conspired.
On the last day of the month, they prepared a sacrifice.
Xú shì cried and expressed her grief to the fullest extent.
After it was finished, she took off her mourning clothes, fumigated herself with incense, and bathed.
Then, in another room, she set up curtains and drapes.
She spoke and laughed joyfully,
showing no sign of sorrow.
Everyone, young and old, was filled with grief.
They were astonished at her behavior.
They secretly observed and watched her,
finding nothing suspicious.
Xú called out to Gāo Yīng and all the maids, spreading them throughout the house.
She sent someone to inform Lǎn, saying that she had finished the mourning and had good luck now,
only waiting for Lord Fǔjūn's orders.
Lǎn entered, full of enthusiasm.
Xú came out of the door to greet Lǎn with a bow.
Just as he completed one bow,
Xú loudly shouted, "The two lords can rise!"
Gāo Yīng and the others came out together.
Together, they killed Lǎn.
The rest of the people immediately went outside to kill Lǎn's staff.
The lady then returned,
wearing mourning clothes, and offered Lǎn's staff's head as a sacrifice at Yì's tomb.
The whole army was shocked,
considering it a divine miracle.
The Lord of Wú subsequently arrived,
and exterminated Lǎn's staff and remaining associates.
"Wúlì" (The History of Wu)
Wú Zǐ, seeking to leave.
She was the wife of Pèi Gōng's grandson, Qùbìng,
and the daughter of Dài Yuánshì from the same commandery.
Having been married for a long time without a child,
she said to her husband:
"I am untalented
to serve you with towel and comb.
Over the years, I have not produced an heir.
The rites have seven reasons for divorce.
Please allow me to receive my dismissal."
Her husband did not allow it.
She further said:
"No blessing is greater than prosperity and flourishing;
no misfortune is greater than having no descendants.
If you cannot bear to dismiss me,
you should take another wife."
Her husband still refused.
After her husband died and the mourning period was over,
her parents wanted to remarry her,
but the woman then took a knife and cut off her nose.
The commandery honored her gate.

Yuǎn Lǜ [Yuǎn Lǜ]
Lǐ Héng, zì Shūpíng, Lǐ Héng, courtesy name Shūpíng,
Xiāngyáng rén, was a native of Xiāngyáng.
Xí Zhú yǐ Nǚ Yīng xí pèi zhī. Xí Zhú used his daughter Nǚ Yīng to betroth to him.
During the Wú 吳 dynasty, when Sūn Xiū 孫休 was the Prefect of Dānyáng 丹陽, he relocated to Dānyáng 丹陽.
Héng 衡 repeatedly used the law to cut him off.
Yīng Xí 英習 often advised him, saying:
"Being lowly and insulting the noble,
being distant and creating discord among relatives,
these are ways to invite disaster."
Héng 衡 did not listen.
It happened that Sūn Liàng 孫亮 was deposed.
Héng 衡 entered from the gate.
Yīng Xí 英習 met him and asked,
"Why do you have a fearful look?
Is the King of Lángyá 琅邪 enthroned?"
Héng 衡 said,
"Yes.
Not listening to your words
has led to this."
Thereupon, he gathered his household guests, intending to flee to Wèi 魏.
Yīng Xí 英習 firmly advised him, saying:
"You must not!
You were originally a commoner.
The late emperor promoted you beyond your due.
You have repeatedly acted impolitely and lacked foresight.
Now you are again suspicious and want to escape and seek survival.
If you return north in this way,
what face will you have to meet the people of the Central Plains?"
Héng 衡 said,
"What plan can you suggest?"
Yīng Xí 英習 said,
"Wáng Lángyé (琅邪王) has always favored goodness and admired fame.
Now that he has just taken office, he wishes to make himself known throughout the world.
He will certainly not kill you out of personal resentment; this is clear.
If you are still uncertain,
you can imprison yourself and go to the prison, submitting a memorial detailing the previous events.
If you openly seek punishment for your crime in this way,
you will instead be treated with leniency and generosity.
It will not only mean survival."
Héng (衡) followed his advice.
Indeed, the king issued an order, saying:
"The Prefect of Dānyáng (丹陽), Lǐ Héng (李衡),
due to suspicions about past events,
has voluntarily surrendered himself to the authorities.
The story of 'shooting the hook' and 'severing the foot covering' demonstrates that
loyalty lies in serving the ruler.
Send Héng (衡) back to his commandery,
and do not let him be doubtful."
He was further appointed as General Wēiyuǎn (威遠將軍),
and granted the ornamental halberd and lance.
Whenever Héng (衡) wanted to manage family affairs,
Yīng Xí (英習) would not listen.
Héng (衡) often quoted the Grand Historian,
mentioning the thousand orange trees in Jiānglíng (江陵),
which would be enough to ennoble your family.
Yīng Xí (英習) said:
"People should worry about lacking virtue and righteousness,
not about being poor.
If one is noble and yet able to be poor, that is truly good.
"Ér yòng cǐ hé wéi?" "What do you use this for?"

When the matter became urgent, she sought repentance from Chóu Chán Shī.
The Chán Master already knew
and said to Liǔ Shì:
"Madam, because of your jealousy,
you previously cut off the maid's finger, thus losing a finger.
And then you cut off the maid's tongue.
Now you are about to have your own tongue severed.
If you repent with all your heart,
then you can be spared."
Liǔ Shì prostrated herself and begged for forgiveness for seven days.
The Chán Master ordered her to open her mouth and chanted over her.
Two snakes emerged from her mouth,
each over a foot long.
He quickly chanted over them,
and they fell to the ground.
Her tongue was also restored to normal.
From then on, she was no longer jealous.
From *Qiān Zǎi*.
Granted Wine.
In the early Táng dynasty,
the Minister of War, Rèn Guī,
was given palace women by imperial decree, all of whom were of exceptional beauty.
A wife's jealousy.
She burned and ruined the hair of two girls until they were bald.
Tàizōng heard of it.
He ordered Shànggōng to bring gold, sesame cakes, and wine to reward her,
saying:
"Drinking this will cause instant death.
Guī deserves the rank of third grade.
It is fitting that he have concubines.
If you are not jealous, then you need not drink it;
if you are jealous, then drink it."
Madam Liǔ bowed and accepted the imperial decree, finishing it,
and said:
"I and Guī have been husband and wife since our hair was bound in marriage.
We both came from humble beginnings,
supporting and assisting each other,
ultimately achieving high official rank.
Now Guī has many inner favorites.
Truly, it would be better for me to die."
Thereupon she drank it all.
However, it was not poison.
After she woke up from sleep,
the emperor said to Guī:
"Her nature is like this;
I too must fear her."
Consequently, he decreed for the two girls
to be settled in separate residences.
*Qiānzǎi*.
*Guó Shǐ Yì Zuǎn*: Fáng Xuánlíng's affair was similar.
Three Things to be Feared
During the reign of Emperor Zhōngzōng (中宗) of the Táng dynasty, the Censor-in-chief, Péi Tán (裴談), revered Buddhism.
His wife was fierce and jealous,
and Péi Tán (裴談) feared her as if she were a strict father.
He once said of his wife that there were three things to be feared:
When she was young and beautiful,
he viewed her as a living Bodhisattva.
Who wouldn't fear a living Bodhisattva?
And when children filled the house,
he viewed her as the Hárītī (訶梨帝母), the mother of nine demon children.
Who wouldn't fear the Hárītī (訶梨帝母), the mother of nine demon children?
And when she was in her fifties or sixties,
lightly applying makeup,
sometimes green, sometimes black,
he viewed her as a Kumbhāṇḍa (鳩盤茶).
Who wouldn't fear a Kumbhāṇḍa (鳩盤茶)?
At that time, the deposed Consort Wéi (韋庶人) greatly imitated the style of Empress Wǔ (武氏),
and Zhōngzōng (中宗) gradually feared her.
At an inner court banquet, while singing the "Huíbō" (廽波) song, a court jester recited a verse saying:
"Huíbō (廽波) at that time, the old woman was afraid of her husband.
The outside is very good,
only Péi Tán (裴談) on the inside is worse off than old Lǐ (李)."
Empress Wéi (韋后) was pleased with herself
and rewarded him with a bolt of silk.
*Běnshì Shī* (本事詩).
The affair of Rèn Guī (任瓌) of the Censorate was similar.
Cutting off ears and noses.
During the Zhōngzōng reign, Princess Yíchéng's (宜城公主) husband, Péi Xùn (裴巽), had an affair with another woman.
The princess sent a eunuch to castrate him.
She had the man seized, his ears cut off, and his nose mutilated.
His scrotal skin was peeled off.
And plastered on the face of her husband,
also cutting off his hair.
She ordered those in the hall handling cases and assembled officials to observe this together.
Both the princess and her husband were impeached at the same time.
The princess was demoted to a county princess.
And her husband was demoted and transferred to a lower position.
*Qiānzǎi* (《僉載》)
Carved Eyebrows.
Fáng Rúfù's (房孺復) wife, Lady Cuī (崔氏), was very jealous.
The maids around her were not allowed to wear heavy makeup or high hairstyles.
She provided them with only one *dòu* of rouge and one *qián* of powder per month.
There was a maid who had recently bought makeup that was slightly better.
Lady Cuī angrily said to her:
"You like makeup, do you?
I will do your makeup for you."
Thereupon, she had her eyebrows carved and filled with blue ink.
She heated the lock beam and branded the corners of both her eyes.
The skin curled up and burned at the touch.
She then applied red pigment to it.
When the scabs fell off, it looked like makeup.
*Yǒuyáng* (《酉陽》)
Yuè qián zhǐ diǎn
(Moon Coin and Paper Dots): Nowadays, women use huā zǐ (floral appliqués) as facial ornaments,
originating from the Zhāoróng (Imperial Concubine) created by Shàngguān Shì,
to cover blemishes.
Before the Dàlì era, many scholar-official couples were jealous and fierce.
If concubines and maids displeased them even slightly, they would brand their faces,
Guǐ (癸) means to measure.
It means measuring and planning before bringing forth life.
The *Erya*
says: Guǐ (癸) means returning.
In the Five Elements, it belongs to Water.
In the Five Phases, it belongs to Fire.
For year names,
when the Tàisuì (太歲) is in Yín (寅), it is called Shè tí gé (攝提格);
when in Mǎo (卯), it is called Dān yān (單閼);
when in Chén (辰), it is called Zhí xú (執徐);
when in Sì (巳), it is called Dà huāng luò (大荒落);
when in Wǔ (午), it is called Dūn zāng (敦牂);
when in Wèi (未), it is called Xié qià (恊洽);
when in Shēn (申), it is called Tūn tān (涒灘);
when in Yǒu (酉), it is called Zuò è (作噩);
when in Xū (戊), it is called Yān mào (閹茂);
when in Hài (亥), it is called Dà yuān xiàn (大淵獻);
when in Zǐ (子), it is called Kùn dūn (困敦);
when in Chǒu (丑), it is called Chì fèn ruò (赤奮若).
Shè tí gé (攝提格)
Lǐ Xún's (李巡) commentary on the *Erya* says:
All things receive Yang and rise,
therefore it is called Shè tí gé (攝提格), meaning rising.
Kǒng Wénxiáng (孔文祥) said that because the year is in Yín (寅),
and the first month comes out of the east,
it is the beginning of all stars,
and uses the Shè tí (攝提) constellation,
therefore it is called Shè tí (攝提),
because it is the head of the years and months,
starting from the first month of spring,
therefore it is called Gé (格), meaning correct.
The *Suǒ yǐn* says:
hence the terms "moon dots" and "coin dots".

Tóng xì
(Servant Play): When Cuī Xuán was in Huáinán,
he once had musicians teach his household servants various plays. One day, the musician reported that they had mastered them
and requested a performance.
Xuán ordered them to perform below the hall,
and he and his wife, Lǐ Shì, sat to watch.
The servants, knowing Lǐ Shì's jealousy,
had several servants dress in women's clothing, designating them as "wife" and "concubines" on either side.
One servant held a tablet and wore a belt,
constantly agreeing and obeying among them,
playing music and ordering wine,
laughing and talking, inevitably showing intention.
Lǐ Shì did not initially understand.
As the play continued,
it completely resembled Lǐ Shì's usual behavior.
Although Lǐ Shì began to realize,
she thought it was just a coincidence,
secretly believing they wouldn't dare,
and continued to watch.
Tóng's (僮) intention was to elicit enlightenment,
so Yù (愈) playfully teased him even more.
Lǐ Guǒ (李果) angrily scolded him, saying:
"How dare you be so rude, you slave?
Have I ever been like this?"
Tóng (僮) pointed at him and rebuked, saying:
"Tsk, tsk, red eyes!
Now you feign ignorance with white eyes!"
Xuàn (鉉) laughed loudly,
almost collapsing with laughter.
*Yùquán Zǐ* (《玉泉子》)
She pierced with an iron awl.
Mǐn Wáng (閩王) Yánhàn's (延翰) wife, Cuī Shì (崔氏),
Yánhàn (延翰) often chose daughters from good families as concubines.
Cuī Shì (崔氏) was by nature jealous.
The more beautiful daughters from good families she always confined to a separate room,
restrained with heavy shackles,
carved wooden figures,
and struck their faces with her hands,
and pierced them with iron awls.
Eighty-four people died.
*Wǔdài Shǐ* (《五代史》)
Hàn's (翰) wife, the daughter of the Bólíng (博陵) clan,
was by nature fierce, jealous, and cruel.
She once bound a serving girl with silk and whipped her
until the silk was dyed red with blood, and only then would she stop.
She also had wooden paddles made to slap people.
Once, in the height of summer,
though the sky was without a trace of clouds, thunder and lightning struck,
Bólíng (博陵) died in the middle of the courtyard.
*Wǔ Guó Gùshì* (五國故事)
Granted silver and colored silk.
The Minister of the Ministry of War, Dù Yè (杜業), was appointed to the Privy Council.
He was resourceful and adaptable,
quick to seize opportunities.
Military affairs, taxes, and population registers
were at his fingertips.
His wife, Zhāng Shì (張氏), was extremely jealous and fierce.
The house had no concubines or maids.
Yè (業) feared her as if she were a strict parent.
Emperor Lièzǔ (烈祖) often ordered Empress Yuán (元皇后) to summon Zhāng (張) to the inner court to admonish her, saying:
"Yè's (業) position and reputation are prominent.
He is entitled to have concubines.
Why are you so restrictive?
Is this what a wife should do?"
Zhāng (張), weeping, said:
"Yè (業) was originally a wild student.
He encountered the holy fortune.
At the beginning of many difficulties,
what Your Majesty relied upon was merely an exhausted nag.
Moreover, he is prematurely aging and often sick.
Indulging him will surely bring him trouble
and may lead to mistakes in his duties."
Emperor Lièzǔ (烈祖) heard this
He greatly praised and admired him,
and rewarded him with a silver basin and colored silk.
*Nán Táng Jìn Shì*
It is said that the maid
Chén Jué served as a guest of Sòng Qíqiū when he was of humble status.
When he became Vice Minister of the Ministry of War,
his wife, Lǐ Shì, was jealous and fierce.
She personally managed the kitchen
and did not keep concubines.
Qíqiū selected three of his own maids and gave them to her.
Lǐ showed no displeasure,
and treated the three maids with the respect due to her parents-in-law.
When people asked her why,
Lǐ said,
"These are people favored by His Excellency (Lìng Gōng).
Seeing them is like seeing His Excellency in person.
How would I dare be disrespectful?"
The three maids felt uneasy,
and requested to return to Sòng's residence.
Sòng smiled and granted their request.
The emperor himself
said that the jealousy of women is especially strange.
Forty years ago, there was a wine supervisor named Fàn, a vice director in Fǔzhōu, whose wife was beautiful but jealous.
Fàn indulged and feared her.
Whenever his colleagues had leave and invited prostitutes for feasts, he was never allowed to participate.
One night, Fàn Lún 范輪 was on duty for the night shift.
Someone came to report someone brewing (wine) for lodging.
Early in the morning, Fàn 范 led his officials and soldiers directly to search and arrest (the brewer).
His colleague, a Lǐ Gòngfèng 李供奉, knew that Fàn's 范 wife was jealous.
He playfully took a prostitute's shoe and secretly placed it in Fàn's 范 bedding.
After a short while, a clerk carried the quilt and bedding back (to Fàn's house).
The wife unfolded the quilt and found the shoe.
Her expression was dejected.
She questioned where it came from.
The clerk said he didn't know.
Thereupon, she wept in resentment.
After a long time, she clutched her chest and cried out,
"Heavens, is this true?"
Then she went into her room, closed the door, and lay down to sleep.
Shortly thereafter, Fàn 范 returned.
He pushed the door open and entered, only to find that she had hanged herself.
"Dùnzhāi Xiánlǎn" 《遯齋閑覽》
Blade
There was someone named (rèn) 任 who served as the deputy magistrate of Húnán 湖南.
His wife had given birth to a son, who was already a year old.
The couple loved and cherished him very much.
One day, the prefect was present.
He told the deputy magistrate (rèn) 任 to administer the affairs of the prefecture.
It happened that the prefect of a neighboring prefecture passed by.
The prefecture held a banquet and ordered courtesans to attend.
Among the courtesans, there was one particularly beautiful and intelligent one who stood by the deputy magistrate (rèn)'s 任 side.
The deputy magistrate (rèn) 任 turned to speak with her.
As they were jesting over wine,
and the laughter and talk were at their height,
suddenly a messenger carrying two platters of raw meat placed them before the host and guests.
The vice prefect, surprised, asked the reason for this.
It was said to be the flesh of her son.
It turned out that the wife, enraged that her husband was talking with prostitutes,
had personally murdered her son,
cutting up his flesh to present to them.
Her poisonous cruelty reached this point!
Above,
the Seven Grounds for Divorce.
Confucius said that there are five kinds of women one should not marry:
one from a family that goes against social norms,
one from a disorderly family,
one whose family has a history of criminals,
one with a family history of loathsome disease,
one who is fatherless,
and the eldest daughter.
A wife can be divorced for seven reasons, but there are three cases in which she cannot be divorced.
The seven grounds for divorce are:
disobedience to her parents-in-law,
being childless,
being lewd,
being jealous,
having a loathsome disease,
being gossipy,
and being a thief.
The "Three Not to Divorce"
refers to circumstances where there is nowhere else for the wife to go;
where she has mourned for the husband's parents for three years;
and where she was poor and lowly when married, but the husband later became rich and honored.
All these are reasons why the sages followed the natural order of relations between men and women,
and valued the beginning of marriage.
Three Generations Divorcing Wives
It began with Shū Liáng Hé 出妻 divorcing his wife.
Bó Yú also divorced his wife,
and Zǐ Sī also divorced his wife.
Therefore, it is said that the Kǒng 孔 family divorced wives for three generations.
*Family Sayings, Postface*
Steamed Goosefoot
Zēng Zǐ's 曾子 stepmother treated him unkindly,
yet his support and care for her did not diminish.
When his wife served goosefoot that was not properly steamed,
he divorced her because of it.
People said this was not one of the Seven Grounds for Divorce.
*Family Sayings*
says:
"I have heard it said
that a relationship ended can become one of friendship,
and a divorced wife can remarry.
It was simply that the goosefoot was not properly steamed;
why question the reason?"
*Bái Hǔ Tōng*
Disliking Failure
Mèngzǐ disliked failure and divorced his wife;
it can be said he was able to strengthen himself.
. "Xúnzi's Explanation of Blindness"
notes:
"He disliked her failing in virtue and so divorced his wife."
Choosing Dates over a Wife
When Wáng Jí was young and studying in Cháng'ān,
the neighbor to the east had a large jujube tree
whose branches hung over Jí's courtyard.
Jí's wife took jujubes to feed Jí.
Later, Jí found out about this and divorced his wife.
The neighbor to the east heard of this and wanted to cut down the tree,
but the neighbors stopped him.
They earnestly requested Jí to take his wife back.
The villagers made a saying for him:
"The neighbor to the east has a tree,
Wáng Yáng divorced his wife.
The neighbor's dates are gone,
he took his wife back."
Such was his determined will.
"Book of Han"
Separation
Lǐ Chōng and his six brothers were so poor that they had no grain stored,
changing clothes to go out,
After eating all day,
his wife secretly said to Chōng 充:
"Now that we are so poor,
I have some private property.
We can divide it and live separately.
With so many people, expenses are extreme,
there's no point in suffering for nothing."
Chōng 充 asked to summon the neighbors and their families to face each other and part ways.
His wife believed him,
and summoned all the neighbors and relatives.
Chōng 充 then knelt forward and reported his wife's words to his mother,
and expelled his wife.
His wife wept and left.
*Rǔnán Jì* 《汝南記》
Disciple Dismisses Wife
Huán Róng 桓榮, at the age of forty, had no children.
His senior disciple, Hé Tāng 何湯, then dismissed Róng's 桓榮 wife to marry another,
who bore him three sons.
Róng 桓榮 greatly valued them.
Xiè Chéng's 謝承 *Hòu Hànshū* 《後漢書》
Mother-in-law Hates and Sends Away
Yīng Shùn 應順, styled Huázhòng 華仲,
was a native of Nándùn 南頓, Rǔnán 汝南,
and served his great-grandfather.
His wife was originally the former wife of Dèng Yuányì 鄧元義 of Rǔnán 汝南.
Yuányì's 鄧元義 father, Bó Kǎo 伯考, was a *shàngshū púsè* 尚書僕射 (vice director of the Department of State Affairs).
Yuán Yì returned to his hometown.
His wife, having stayed behind, served her mother-in-law with utmost diligence.
The mother-in-law resented her.
She confined her in an empty room,
restricting her food and drink.
Weak and exposed, she suffered more each day.
Yet the wife never uttered a word of complaint.
Later, her husband's elder brother, moved by suspicion, inquired about it.
At that time, Yì's son, Lǎng, was several years old.
He said that his mother was not ill,
but only suffered from hunger.
The elder brother burst into tears and said:
"Who would have thought that our own aunt would be the cause of such suffering!"
He sent her back to her family and remarried her to Huá Zhòng as his wife.
Zhòng was the Director of Works.
His wife rode in a court carriage one morning.
Yuán Yì watched her by the roadside.
He said to someone:
"This is my former wife.
She was without any fault.
It was that her husband's family treated her so cruelly.
They should have valued each other."
At the time, his son Lǎng was a court gentleman.
His mother sent letters to him, but he never replied.
If she gave him clothes, he would immediately burn them.
His mother did not mind it.
Wishing to see him,
she went to the ancestral hall of her current husband's family, the Lǐ family.
He had someone use other words to request Lǎng to come.
Lǎng arrived and saw his mother.
He bowed twice, weeping.
Thereupon, he stood up and left his mother.
He turned back and said to her,
"I almost died.
I thought I had been abandoned by your family.
What crimes or transgressions have I committed
that you treat me like this?"
Consequently, he broke off the relationship.
*Rǔnán Jì*
Scolding the Dog
Bào Yǒng, styled Jūnzhǎng,
was ambitious and virtuous from a young age.
He served his stepmother with utmost filial piety.
Once, his wife scolded the dog in front of his mother,
and Yǒng immediately divorced her.
*Hòu Hàn*
Upstream
Jiāng Shī served his mother with utmost filial piety.
His mother liked to drink river water.
His wife once went upstream to fetch water,
but encountered wind and could not get it.
Returning, his mother was thirsty.
Shī scolded her and sent her away.
*Hòu Shū*
Bái Lètiān 白樂天 judged:
"Jiāng Shī's 姜詩 expulsion of his wife
was for a minor flaw.
Bào Yǒng's 鮑永 dismissal of his wife
was also not excessive."
Dòu Xuán 竇玄 was abandoned
due to his exceedingly strange appearance.
The Emperor married a princess to him.
His former wife wrote a letter of farewell to Xuán:
"The abandoned wife respectfully states:
I, Bái Dòu 白竇, am of humble birth.
My lowliness and ugliness are not equal to a noble person.
My relationship with him grows more distant day by day,
while her relationship with him grows closer day by day.
Clothes are never tired of being new,
but people are tired of being old.
The sorrow is unbearable,
the resentment is irremovable.
What kind of person is she
to occupy my place?"
*Hòu Shū* (Book of the Later Han)
Opening the farewell letter,
Sītú Yuán Kuí 司徒袁隗 sought a marriage for his niece.
Upon seeing Huáng Yǔn 黃允, he said:
"To obtain a son-in-law like this is enough."
Yǔn returned home
He divorced his wife, Xiàhóu (夏侯) woman.
His parents said:
"When a woman is divorced,
she should divide her hairpin and cut her belt."
He then returned Yuán Ài (元艾) to be the master,
and invited more than three hundred relatives and guests.
Xiàhóu (夏侯) in the seat raised her arm,
enumerating fifteen hidden and shameful evils of Yǔn (允).
Thereupon, she crossed the mat and boarded the carriage,
and Yǔn (允) was dismissed from his position because of this.
*Hàn Jì* (漢紀)
Losing a Pearl
Lǐ Jìng (李敬) of Rǔnán (汝南) was a slave to the chancellor of Zhào (趙).
He found a strung pearl in a rat's hole,
with dangling ornaments connected to it.
He asked the head clerk about it.
The head clerk replied:
"The former chancellor's wife once lost three pearls,
and suspected that his daughter-in-law had stolen them,
and therefore drove his daughter-in-law away."
Jìng (敬) then sent the pearl to the former chancellor.
The chancellor was ashamed and pursued to bring back his daughter-in-law.
Xiè Chéng's (謝承) *Hòu Hàn Shū* (後漢書)
The Xī (郗) Family's Divorce
Wáng Xiànzhī (王獻之) was seriously ill.
A Taoist priest submitted a memorial to Heaven and should review his faults.
Asking Zǐjìng (子敬) what his differences, similarities, gains, and losses were,
Zǐjìng (子敬) said:
"I don't remember anything else,
I only remember divorcing the Xī (郗) family."
*Shìshuō Xīnyǔ* (世說新語)
Xiànzhī (獻之) married Xī Tán's (郗曇) daughter named Dàomào (道茂).
During the Xiánníng (咸寧) era, he received an imperial edict to marry the Princess of Yúyáo (餘姚公主).
*Bié Zhuàn* (別傳)
Breaking the *míwú* (蘼蕪)
The recluse Liú Huán (劉瓛) lived on Green Dragon Mountain in Shàngyuán (上元).
He was the leader of the scholars.
He served until the age of forty without marrying.
His friends wanted him to marry a woman from the Wáng (王) family.
Thereupon, he went to the stream, broke off *míwú*, and left.
Hence, it was named *Míwú* Stream (蘼蕪澗).
*Jīnlíng Gùshì* (金陵故事)
During the Jiànyuán (建元) era,
Emperor Gāo (高帝) and Sītú (司徒) Chǔ Yànhuí (禇彥回) arranged for Huán (瓛) to marry a woman from the Wáng (王) family.
The woman from the Wáng (王) family made a hole in the wall and hung her shoe,
which fell onto the bed of her mother-in-law, Lady Kǒng (孔氏).
Lady Kǒng (孔氏) was displeased.
Huán (瓛) then divorced his wife.
*Běn Zhuàn* (本傳)
Pleasing the Intention
Cuī Hào (崔顥) passed the *jìnshì* (進士) examination.
He had talent but lacked moral character.
Hǎo Pú enjoyed drinking and
traveling to the capital.
When he married, he chose women with beautiful appearances,
and would abandon them if they didn't please him even slightly.
*Jiù Táng* (Old Book of Tang)
The spirit sued.
Péi Zhāng of Hédōng,
whose father, Cáo, once garrisoned the gate of Jīngzhōu,
the monk Tánzhào was highly virtuous
and could foretell good and bad fortune.
When Zhāng was young, Tánzhào valued him highly,
saying that his rank and position would surpass those of his father.
When Zhāng was just over twenty, his father married him to a woman from the Lǐ family.
When Zhāng was over forty,
Zhāng, following his official duties, went to Tàiyuán.
He abandoned his wife in Luòyáng,
passing by her door without entering,
being infatuated with someone else.
Madam Lǐ, feeling slighted,
always wore a simple robe and tied-up hair, read Buddhist scriptures, and ate vegetarian food.
Ten years later, Yán Shòu, a Director,
moved his garrison from Jīngzhōu to Tàiyuán.
Tánzhào followed him.
Zhāng then saw Tánzhào,
reminisced about the past for a long time,
and said,
"Fifty years ago, this poor monk said that you, sir, would surely be wealthy and noble,
今則皆不，
何也？” Zhāng himself used the matter of his mistreating his wife to initiate the conversation.
Zhāng 自以薄妻之事啟之，
Zhào said,
“Your wife's soul appealed to the God on High,
complaining that she was being unfairly treated by you."
Several days later, the person below used a blade to cut open her abdomen in the bathing vessel,
her five internal organs collapsed, and she died from the resulting wound.
*Nánbù Xīnshū*
She left a poem as a farewell.
During the Tiānyòu reign period, there was a Shèn woman from Qíting,
the daughter of a Confucian scholar.
Sān Shǐ Yán, the husband of Guàn Fū, passed by,
and they married.
They returned together to Qíchūn.
After several years, they had no heir,
so he found fault with her and divorced her.
After the Shèn woman boarded the carriage, she left a poem as a farewell, saying:
"At that time, our hearts were already connected,
but now, like scattered rain and dispersing clouds, it's just a fleeting moment.
Even if a lonely sail departs from here,
it cannot bear to pass again by Wàngfū Mountain."
After reading the poem, he was filled with sorrow and regret,
and so he lived with her until old age.
*Táng Sòng Yíshǐ*
Divorcing the Wife After Death
Wáng Pāng,
was the second son of Ān Shí.
He suffered from a heart ailment.
He married a woman of the Páng family,
but they were not harmonious.
He divorced her and allowed her to remarry.
At that time, Hóu Xiàn died,
and his wife's conduct was improper.
Ān Shí reported the matter and had her expelled.
A contemporary saying went:
"Wáng Tàizhù married off a woman while still alive,
and Minister Hóu divorced his wife after death."
*Juàn Yóu Zá Lù*
Spilt water cannot be gathered.
Tài Gōng Wàng, when he was a young son-in-law to the Mǎ family,
was abandoned when he grew old.
He sold soy sauce in Mèngjīn,
but encountered a spell of extremely cold weather.
He changed his profession to selling noodles,
but then encountered a great wind.
He rented a space in Jíjīn,
but was not hired, despite offering his services.
He butchered cattle in Zhāogē,
but the meat spoiled because of the heat.
Everything he attempted met with misfortune.
Then he fished at Zīquán.
The Earl of the West went hunting,
與語大悅，
loaded him onto his carriage and returned together,
and established him as his teacher.
When King Wǔ of Zhōu pacified the Shāng,
he was enfeoffed in eastern Qí.
On the way to his domain, he encountered a woman,
who wept and questioned him.
She was his former wife.
She bowed twice and begged to be reunited.
The Duke took a basin of water and poured it on the ground,
ordering her to collect it.
She only managed to gather a little mud.
Tàigōng said:
"If you speak of separating and then rejoining,
spilled water is certainly difficult to recover."
The woman then died with resentment.
Now there is the Tomb of Mā Mǔ.
From *Lǚ Lǎn*, *Guó Cè*, *Shuō Yuàn*, *Hán Shī*, *Hé Guānzi*, with annotation by Wáng Péngshòu in *Lèi Lín*.
Mǎ Wǔ said:
"Spilled water cannot be recovered,
what good is regret?"
From *Hòu Jì*.
As Sūn Hào was about to be defeated,
he left a letter to his ministers saying:
"I have failed you all,
the situation is already difficult to plan for,
spilled water cannot be recovered."
From *Jiāng Biǎo Zhuàn* [missing character].
Zhōu Wáng Míngguǎng 周王明廣 said to Wèi Yuánsōng 衛元嵩:
"Dīng Gōng 丁公 entered Hàn 漢.
He first obtained the remnants of the orthodox classics.
Mǎ Mǔ 馬母 rebelled against Jiāng 姜,
and brought upon herself the fate of spilled water."
From the *Guǎng Hóngmíng Jí* 《廣弘明集》.
On the Governance of the Way:
Zhū Mǎichén 朱買臣, styled Wēngzǐ 翁子,
once sold firewood
and would recite books while walking.
His wife, ashamed of him, asked to leave.
Later, Mǎichén walked alone, singing on the road.
His former wife and her husband were visiting graves and saw Mǎichén, hungry and cold.
They called him over to eat.
After Mǎichén became the Grand Administrator of Kuàijī 會稽,
he entered the territory of Wú 吳 and saw his former wife and her husband working on the road.
Mǎichén stopped his carriage and summoned them.
A carriage behind carried the couple to the Grand Administrator's residence.
They were placed in the garden and provided with food.
After a month,
the wife hanged herself.
Reproaching Severely:
Sòng Xú Guǎng 宋徐廣 was from a poor family.
He never concerned himself with family property.
His wife was the daughter of Zhōngshān Liú Mìzhī 中山劉謐之.
She resented this
The calculations were yielded back and forth,
Guǎng ultimately did not change.
It was like this for ten-odd years,
the family's finances daily declined,
Guǎng left.
*Nán Shǐ* Twenty-three
Burning Books
Wáng Huān, styled Jūnhòu,
was a native of Lèlíng.
Content with poverty and delighting in the Dao,
he did not manage any property.
He often begged for food and recited poetry.
Although his family had no measure of stored grain,
his spirit was content.
His wife was troubled by this,
and so burned and destroyed his books, seeking to remarry.
Huān laughed and said to her,
"Have you not heard of Zhū Mǎichén's wife?"
Those who heard this mostly ridiculed him,
but Huān's adherence to his ambition became even firmer,
and eventually he became a well-versed scholar.
*Jìn Shū*
Demanding Books
Yán Zhēnqīng, as the Prefect of Fǔzhōu,
had a local named Yáng Zhìjiān who loved learning but lived in poverty.
His wife, because the financial support was insufficient,
She submitted a petition seeking a divorce.
Zhì Jiān saw her off with a poem, saying:
"In those years, I made up my mind to follow a teacher early on,
But today, it has turned into gray hairs at my temples.
Knowing myself to be ungainly, I realize I sought officialdom late,
Willingly delaying abandoning my body in vain.
Let gold hairpins casually style new hair,
Let the phoenix mirror reflect different painted eyebrows.
From now on, we will be merely fellow travelers,
Meeting again will be like descending from the mountain."
His wife took the poem to the magistrate and requested to marry another man.
Zhēnqīng judged the document, saying:
"Yáng Zhìjiān became familiar with Confucian teachings early on,
And is quite well known for his poetry.
His foolish wife, seeing that he had not yet attained success,
Thus, she has had a mind to leave him.
Now that Wáng Huān's granary is empty,
Will you not respect the yellow scrolls?
Zhū Sǒu's wife must leave,
preferring to see brocade garments?
She acts like Mí Zhuī, the wife of Jì Quē,
Aiding and abetting a good cause,
She only learns from Mǎi Chén's wife,
Lightly abandoning her good husband.
This pollutes the village,
Damages morals and education,
If there is no punishment,
Who will stop the frivolous clamor?
The wife could be beaten twenty times
and allowed to remarry as she pleases.
Yáng Zhìjiān 楊志堅, a Xiùcai 秀才 (a successful candidate in the imperial examination), provided provisions of grain and silk;
he was also appointed to a position in the army.
When this was heard far and wide,
everyone was pleased and convinced.
From then on, no woman in the Jiāngzuǒ 江左 region dared to abandon her husband.
*Yúnxī Yǒuyì* 《雲溪友議》
Giving Pearls
King Fūchāi 夫差 of Wú 吳 had a youngest daughter named Zǐguī 紫珪,
who was both talented and beautiful.
Tóng Zhòngér 童重兒 of the Hán 韓 family desired to marry her,
but the king did not permit it.
Zǐguī 紫珪, swallowing her resentment, died.
Zhòngér 重兒 returned from his studies and learned of this.
Moved by her devotion, he prepared silks and money to mourn before her grave.
Zǐguī's 紫珪 spirit emerged from the tomb,
saw Zhòngér 重兒 and wept.
Together, they returned to the tomb.
For three days and nights, she presented him with a pearl the size of an inch in diameter and a white jade pot,
stretching her neck and singing:
"There are birds on the southern mountain,
nets spread on the northern mountain.
I wished to follow you,
but slanderous words were plentiful.
Grief congealed into disease,
ending my life in the yellow tomb.
My fate is not well-made;
How could I have feathers (wings) to fly away?
The leader of my race is named Fènghuáng (Phoenix);
One day, I lost my male (mate);
For three years, I have felt sorrow and pain.
Although there are many birds,
None can be my matching pair.
Therefore, I keep my humble appearance hidden,
But I have encountered your brilliant light.
Though our bodies are far apart, our hearts are close;
How could I ever forget this moment?"
The *Sōu Shén Jì* ("Records of Spirits and Strange Things") refers to her as Zǐ Yù (Purple Jade).
A prince consort,
Xīn Dàodù of Lǒngxī, was traveling for study.
He was walking to the north, five *lǐ* west of Yōngzhōu city,
and saw a large mansion.
A woman in green clothes was at the gate.
Xīn Dàodù asked the doorkeeper for a meal.
The woman went in and told the Qín woman.
The woman ordered him to be summoned in.
Dàodù hastened into the pavilion.
The Qín woman sat on a western couch.
Dàodù announced his name and finished describing his daily life.
She ordered him to sit on an eastern couch.
Immediately, food and drink were prepared.
After he had eaten,
the woman said to Dàodù:
"I am a princess of the state of Qín,
sent to marry into the state of Cáo.
Unfortunately, I died without a husband.
It has been twenty-three years since my death.
I have been living alone in this house.
Today, you have come,
and I wish to become husband and wife with you."
After three nights and three days,
suddenly the woman said to him:
"You are a living person, and I am a ghost.
Sharing this lodging with you
can only last for three nights.
We cannot stay together for long,
or there will be misfortune.
However, during this short stay,
we have not fully enjoyed our intimacy.
Now that we must part,
how can I give you a token of my love?"
She ordered someone to take the box behind the bed and open it.
She took out a gold pillow
and gave it to Dù as a token.
Then, they parted with tears.
She immediately sent a servant girl in green to escort him out the door.
Before he had taken more than a few steps,
he could no longer see the house.
There was only a grave mound.
Dù, in a state of panic, ran out.
He checked and the gold pillow was in his arms.
There was no further strange occurrence.
He then went to the state of Qín.
He used the pillow to sell it in the market.
It so happened that a concubine of Qín was riding in her carriage on a tour.
She personally saw Dù selling the gold pillow.
Suspicious, she asked to see it.
She asked Dù where he had gotten it.
Dù told her everything in detail.
The concubine, upon hearing this, wept sorrowfully, unable to control herself.
However, she still had doubts.
She then sent people to open the tomb.
They opened the coffin to examine it.
All the burial objects were still there.
Only the gold pillow was missing.
They carefully examined the corpse.
The signs of intimacy were as if it had just happened.
The Qín concubine then believed it.
She sighed and said:
"My daughter Dàshèng died.
Even after twenty-three years, she can still interact with the living.
This is truly my son-in-law."
Consequently, she appointed Dào Dù as a Fùmǎ Dūwèi (駙馬都尉, Imperial Son-in-Law Commandant),
bestowed upon him gold, silk, carriages, and horses,
and ordered him to return to his own country.
From this incident onwards,
later generations called sons-in-law Fùmǎ (駙馬, Imperial Son-in-Law).
Today's imperial sons-in-law are also called Fùmǎ."
From *Sōushén Jì* (搜神記, Records of Searching for the Supernatural)
Regeneration
During the time of Qín Shǐhuáng, there was Wáng Dàopíng,
a native of Cháng'ān.
In his youth, he and Táng Shū, a person from the same village, had a daughter,
whose given name was Fù Yù,
beautiful in both appearance and complexion.
They vowed to become husband and wife.
Soon after, Wáng Dàopíng was conscripted for military service,
and became trapped in the Southern lands,
not returning for nine years.
Her parents, seeing their daughter growing up,
betrothed her to Liú Xiáng as his wife.
The daughter's vows with Dàopíng were very solemn,
and she refused to change her mind.
Her parents pressed her,
and she could not avoid marrying Liú Xiáng.
After three years,
she was constantly unhappy,
always thinking of Dàopíng,
resenting it,
deeply depressed, and died.
Three years after her death,
Dàopíng returned home,
and asked the villagers where this woman was.
The villagers said:
"This woman's heart was with you,
but she was forced by her parents
She married Liú Xiáng 劉祥,
but now he is dead."
Píng 平 asked where her tomb was.
The villagers led him to the tomb.
Píng 平 wailed and choked with sobs,
calling her name three times.
He circled the tomb in sorrow, unable to stop himself.
Then Píng 平 prayed, saying:
"I swore an oath to Heaven and Earth with you,
promising to protect you for life.
Unexpectedly, I was entangled in official matters,
causing us to be separated.
Your parents and Liú Xiáng 劉祥 did not agree with our original intention,
so we are separated forever in life and death.
If you have a divine spirit,
let me see your face as you were in life.
If you have no divine spirit,
then I will depart from here." Having said this,
he wept again, lingering back and forth.
The spirit of the woman emerged from the tomb
and asked Píng 平 where he had come from.
After a long time, they expressed their longing for each other.
"Originally, I swore to be husband and wife with you to ensure our lifelong commitment,
but my father forced me
to marry Liú Xiáng 劉祥.
It has been three years.
I missed you day and night, becoming sick,
harboring resentment, and dying.
Separated by the lonely path to the underworld,
but considering your longstanding desire,
not forgetting to seek solace once more,
my body is undamaged,
I can be reborn,
and we can once again be husband and wife.
Quickly open the tomb,
break open the coffin and take me out – if you doubt my words, examine for yourself.
Thereupon he opened the tomb and felt around to see;
the woman was indeed alive.
So he packed up and followed Wáng Dàopíng back home.
Her husband, Liú Xiáng, heard of this and was astonished.
He reported the matter to the prefecture and county, seeking a judgment in accordance with the law.
But no provision in the law applied.
So he recorded the circumstances and presented them to the king.
The king then ruled that she should be returned to Wáng Dàopíng as his wife.
She lived to the age of one hundred and twenty years.
Truly, it can be said that sincerity can penetrate heaven and earth,
and thus one can obtain such a response.
*Soushen Ji* (In Search of the Supernatural)
During the Yuánkāng era, a woman from Liáng state was promised in marriage.
The betrothal gifts had already been accepted.
Soon after, her husband was sent as a soldier to Cháng'ān.
He did not return for many years.
The woman's family then decided to marry her to another man.
The woman was unwilling to go,
but her parents pressured and forced her.
Unable to resist, she departed,
Eventually, she was found to have died of illness.
Later, her husband returned.
He asked where his daughter was.
Her family members told him about it in detail.
Her husband went directly to his daughter's grave.
Unable to bear his grief,
he then broke open the tomb and opened the coffin.
The daughter then came back to life.
Consequently, he returned home with her.
Later, the second husband heard of this.
He went to the authorities to dispute the matter.
The local authorities were unable to make a decision.
The Secretary Wang Dǎo advised:
"This is an extraordinary matter.
It cannot be judged by ordinary principles.
She should be returned to her former husband."
The court followed his advice.
"Record of the Five Elements of Jin"
Guǐ Zǐ Lú Chōng,
a man from Fànyáng,
Whose home was thirty *lǐ* west of the tomb of Vice Prefect Cuī.
On the day before the Winter Solstice, Chōng went hunting west of his home.
He saw a roe deer.
He drew his bow and shot it, hitting it immediately.
The roe deer fell over but then got up again.
Chōng pursued it unknowingly.
Suddenly, he saw a village gate that resembled a government office.
Suddenly, he saw a gate like that of a mansion a *lǐ* away.
Inside the gate, beneath a bell, was a *chàngjiā* (herald) at the front.
Chōng asked what kind of residence this was.
The reply was: "This is the residence of the Shǎofǔ (Treasurer of the Imperial Household)."
Chōng said, "My clothes are wretched; how could I meet such a noble person?"
Immediately, someone brought a bundle of new clothes to greet him.
Chōng put them on; they fit perfectly.
Then he proceeded to meet the Shǎofǔ.
He presented his name.
After several rounds of wine and roasted meat,
Cuī said, "I recently received a letter from your respected father,
asking for my youngest daughter to marry you.
That is why I have been waiting for you."
He then held up the letter to show Chōng.
Although Chōng was young when his father died,
he had seen his father's handwriting before.
He then sobbed, speechless.
Cuī immediately ordered the inner palace to have the young lady dress up and have Chōng go to the east corridor.
Chōng arrived, and the bride had already gotten out of the carriage.
They stood at the head of the mat and bowed together.
After three days, the ceremony was complete, and he returned to see Cuī.
Cuī said, "You may return home now.
Your wife has the signs of pregnancy.
If she gives birth to a son, he should be returned to me.
If she gives birth to a daughter, she should be kept and raised by yourselves."
He ordered those outside to prepare a carriage to escort the guest.
Cuī escorted him to the gate,
held his hand, and shed tears.
The feeling of parting was no different from parting with a living person.
He again presented her with a set of clothes,
and a set of bedding,
to make it convenient for her to board the carriage.
She left as swiftly as lightning.
In a short while, he arrived home.
His family members met him,
and, filled with mixed sorrow and joy, eagerly inquired about his experiences.
They learned that Cuī (崔) was a deceased person who had entered her tomb,
and they expressed their regret and lamentation.
After living there for four years,
on the third day of the third month, he was playing by the water.
Suddenly, he saw a small ox-cart alternately floating and sinking.
Once it reached the shore,
Chōng (充) went to open the back door of the cart and saw a Miss Cuī (崔氏) and a three-year-old boy riding together.
Chōng (充) was delighted to see them and
wanted to take her hand,
but the woman raised her finger and pointed to the back of the cart, saying:
"If the Fǔjūn (府君) sees people, the Shǎofǔ (少府) will also see them."
Chōng (充) went to inquire,
but the woman hugged the child and returned.
Chōng (充) then bid farewell to the gold and also presented her with a poem, saying:
"Bright is the substance of the spiritual zhī (芝),
its radiance and beauty, how magnificent!
It manifested in Huáyīn (華陰) back then,
its auspicious strangeness displaying its divinity.
Containing its essence, it did not reach full bloom,
in midsummer, it suffered frost and withered.
Glory fades into darkness,
worldly paths offer no application.
Not understanding the workings of yin and yang,
a wise person suddenly appears.
Meetings are shallow, separations are swift,
all due to the spirits.
What can I give my loved ones?
Golden *kě* pendants for the child.
Love and kindness, from now on, we part,
a severance that wounds liver and spleen."
Chōng took the child and the poem,
and suddenly could not see where the two carts had gone.
He returned the child to the assembled people,
who all shook their heads, thinking it was a ghost or demon,
and spat on it, but its form remained as before.
They asked the child, "Who is your father?"
The child went directly into Chōng's arms.
At first, everyone thought it strange and evil,
but then they circulated and examined the poem,
and sighed with emotion at the mysterious communication between life and death.
Chōng went to the market to sell it,
raising its price high,
not wanting to sell it quickly,
hoping for someone who would recognize its value.
Suddenly, an old maidservant asked Chōng how he had obtained it,
and went back to report to her master,
who was the woman's aunt.
She sent someone to look, and indeed it was the item.
Wèi Chōng said to him:
"My aunt's elder sister was the daughter of Prefect Cui Shàofǔ,
she died before she was married.
Her family grieved for her,
and buried her with golden chopsticks in her coffin.
Now looking at you, you greatly resemble her,
may I learn the whole story?"
Chōng responded with the details of the matter.
She then went to Chōng's house to welcome the child.
The child had the appearance of the Cui family,
and also resembled Chōng.
The aunt said:
"My maternal uncle and this child were born around the end of the third month."
The father said:
"This spring was warm,
I wish to name him Wēnxiū."
He then named him Wēnxiū.
Wēnxiū was indeed a 'ghost marriage' child,
the omen of which had already been revealed.
The child then became an excellent talent,
serving as the administrator of several commanderies with two-thousand-dan salaries,
all with outstanding achievements.
Later, he had a son named Zhí,
who became a Shangshu (Secretary) in the Hàn dynasty.
Zhí's son, Yù, became a Sīkōng (Minister of Works) in the Wèi dynasty,
and distinguished officials have succeeded each other to this day.
*Zhì Guài* (A Record of Anomalies)
Lìang Shānbó and Zhù Yīngtái, classmates,
were both people of the Eastern Jìn Dynasty.
The Lìang family was from Kuàijī,
the Zhù family was from Shàngyú.
They once studied together.
Zhù returned home before Lìang.
Later, Lìang passed through Shàngyú
to visit her,
and only then did he realize she was a woman.
Upon returning home, he told his parents
and wanted to marry her, but
she had already been promised to the son of the Mǎ family.
Lìang was filled with melancholy and a sense of loss.
Three years later, Lìang became the magistrate of Yín and died from illness,
leaving instructions to be buried at the foot of Qīngdào Mountain.
The following year, Zhù married into the Mǎ family,
and when passing by that place,
a great storm arose,
and the boat could not move forward.
Zhù then went to Lìang's tomb,
crying with a piercing voice.
Suddenly, the ground split open,
and Zhù threw herself in and died there.
The Mǎ family reported this matter to the court.
The Chancellor Xiè Ān requested that she be honored as a virtuous woman.
During the reign of Emperor Hé, Lìang again manifested miraculous powers,
rendering service to the country.
He was ennobled as the Loyal and Righteous,
The officials established a temple in Yín 鄞,
saying that in Wú 吳 there was a "flower butterfly,"
transformed from the citrus fruit borer.
Women and children call it Liáng Shānbó 梁山伯 and Zhù Yīngtái 祝英臺.
*Níngbō Zhì* 《寧波志》.
Tomb of the Goddess
During the reign of the Shào Emperor 紹 of Sòng 宋, a scholar from Nánxú 南徐 was traveling from Mount Huà 華 to Yúnyáng 雲陽.
He saw a woman in a guesthouse
and was delighted by her, but had no means [to approach her],
and consequently fell ill with lovesickness.
His mother asked him the reason,
and he told her everything.
The mother went to find the woman,
and explained the situation to her in detail.
The woman was touched by it,
so she took off her *bìxī* 蔽膝 (a type of apron),
and instructed the mother to secretly hide it under the mat,
and sleeping on it would cure him.
After several days, he indeed recovered.
Suddenly, he lifted the mat and saw the *bìxī* 蔽膝,
held it and wept until his breath was about to stop,
and said to his mother,
"When they bury me, go past Mount Huà 華."
The mother followed his wish,
and went north to the woman's door.
The ox refused to move.
After waiting a moment,
The woman completed her makeup and bathing, then went out and sang,
"At the foot of Mount Huàshān, you have died for me,
for whom else should I live alone?
If you pity me,
let the coffin open for me."
Having spoken,
the coffin opened,
and the woman then went into the coffin,
and they were buried together.
It was called the Tomb of the Divine Woman.
From *Cānchá Zi*.
Rebirth:
During the Kāiyuán reign (713-741), the daughter of Zhāng Guǒ of Zheng Prefecture, formerly the Sīmǎ (司馬) of Yì Prefecture, died.
She was temporarily buried under the pavilion.
Liú Yǐ came to replace him,
and his son often stayed in the pavilion.
At dusk, a beautiful woman came,
and they became intimate.
After several months,
she suddenly said to Liú:
"I am the daughter of the former Sīmǎ Zhāng,
who was buried uncoffined in this pavilion.
My fate dictates that I shall be reborn.
After three days of being intimate with you,
you can see the hair at the place where I am healed and leave."
Liú opened the coffin as planned,
and by the next morning, she had been revived.
Gradually she was able to speak.
After several days, she could sit up and get out of bed.
Her father went to the pavilion and saw his daughter there.
He asked and learned the reason for it.
Thereupon, he sobbed and said:
"This is a divinely appointed time of utmost influence.
Why conceal it?"
Consequently, he sent word to Guǒ [果] to request the marriage.
Her parents were astonished and delighted.
They kept the appointment and the marriage was consummated.
This fine couple later produced several sons.
From *Guǎng Yì Jì* ("Extensive Records of the Strange")
Ghost Embryo
It is said that Dài [代] stated that Zhèng Tián [鄭畋] was a ghost embryo.
After his mother died, his father Yà [亞] remarried and Tián [畋] was born.
Initially, Yà [亞] was not successful,
traveling to various places.
He left his wife and a maidservant at the side of the nunnery in the mountain temple.
When he returned, his wife had already died.
He asked the maidservant,
and the maidservant said:
"Madam was about to give birth,
she lay down,
and in the evening, she heard a voice in the air saying:
'You must go outside the temple,
do not defile my pure place,
otherwise, I will kill you.'"
His wife prayed, saying:
"I am a woman,
with nowhere to return to.
I hope the sage will have pity on me."
At the break of dawn,
after childbirth, she died within the Daoist temple.
The Daoist priests had her buried outside the wall in a field.
Yà used money and wine to offer sauce at her grave.
That night, he dreamed his wife said:
"My life is not yet over.
I am destined to have a noble son with you.
But because I defiled the Daoist temple,
I was killed by the spirits.
Ten *lǐ* south from here is a Buddhist temple.
There is only one monk there,
about fifty years old.
He is an extraordinary person.
You should go and seek him out.

The next year, during the Qingming Festival,

The gate and courtyard were as before,

"Last year today, within this gate,
A face and peach blossoms, reflecting each other in crimson.

Several days later, he went again,

He asked about it,
and the old father said:

Cuī asked to enter and mourn her.
She was still lying on the bed, appearing lifelike.
Cuī raised her head and pillowed it on his thigh, saying:

Ruǎn Diànfū, of Lújiāng, Hé Huī, had a courtesan named Zhāng Yào Huá,
beautiful and favored.
As the governor of Guǎngzhōu was about to depart,
he invited Diànfū to drink.
He set up music and saw that Zhāng was pleasing,
and repeatedly asked Huī, saying:
"Huī can be obtained,
but this person cannot."
Diànfū flung his sleeves and went out the door, saying:
"Is it a case of regretting losing a finger but losing the whole palm?"
He then persuaded the authorities
to impeach Huī on official matters.
From *Nán Shǐ Ēn Xìng Zhuàn* (History of the South: Biographies of Favored Subjects)
Xú Yuè Huá
After the death of Gāoyáng Prince Yōng,
all the courtesans were ordered to become nuns,
or some were married off.
The beauty Xú Yuè Huá was skilled at playing the harp (kōnghóu)
and could perform the song "Míng Fēi Leaving the塞 Border."
Those who heard her sing were all moved.
During the Yǒng'ān era, she became a concubine of General of the Guard Yuán Shìkāng.
Her residence was near Qīngyáng Gate.
Xú played the harp and sang,
her mournful voice reaching the clouds.
Those walking on the road, listening, quickly formed a market (a crowd gathered).
Xú Cháng 徐常 spoke to Shì Kāng 士康, saying:
"The King has two beautiful concubines.
One is named Xiūróng 修容, the other Yànzī 艷姿.
Both have moth eyebrows and white teeth,
with pure appearances that could topple cities.
Xiūróng 修容 can also perform the *Lǜshuǐ Gē* 綠水歌 song,
and Yànzī 艷姿 is skilled in the *Huǒfèng Wǔ* 火鳳舞 Phoenix Dance.
They both are deeply loved within the inner chambers
and their favor exceeds all the other concubines."
Shì Yuán 士原 heard this
and consequently often ordered Xú 徐 to play the *Lǜshuǐ* 綠水 and *Huǒfèng* 火鳳 melodies.
*Luòyáng Qiélán Jì* 洛陽伽藍記 (Records of the Buddhist Monasteries of Luoyang)
Zhāoyún 朝雲
Héjiān Wáng Chēn 河間王琛 had three hundred female entertainers,
all of whom were of exceptional beauty.
There was a maid named Zhāoyún 朝雲,
who was skilled in playing the *chí* 箎 (bamboo flute).
She was favored for singing *Lǒngshàng Shēng* 隴上聲 (Tunes from Longshang) accompanied by a round fan.
When Chēn 琛 served as the Prefect of Qínzhōu 秦州,
the various Qiāng 羗 tribes rebelled.
He repeatedly attacked them, but they did not surrender.
Chēn 琛 ordered Zhāoyún 朝雲 to disguise herself as a poor old woman,
playing the *chí* 箎 while begging.
The Qiāng 羗 tribes heard it,
and all shed tears,
They said to each other,
"Why abandon our graves and wells to become bandits in the mountains?"
And so they led each other to surrender.
The people of Qín said,
"A swift horse and a strong soldier
are not as good as an old woman playing the bamboo flute."

Chūnfēng
In the Shangāo ward of Luòyáng, there was the residence of General Guō Wényuǎn, the Champion.
Its halls, buildings, gardens, and forests
were comparable to those of a feudal lord.
At that time, Lǒngxī's Lǐ Yuánqiān enjoyed using double initial (alliterative) expressions.
He often passed by the front of Wényuǎn's residence.
Passing by, he saw that its gate and facade were splendid and beautiful.
Thereupon he said,
"Whose residence is excessively fine?"
The maid Chūnfēng came out and said,
"The home of Guō, the Champion."
Yuánqiān said,
"All the maids speak in double initials."
Chūnfēng said,
"You, laggard, are slow to scold."
Yuánqiān admired the maid's ability,
and thus the capital city enthusiastically spread the story.

Zǐguāng
Yuán Zhàn's name and position gradually became important.
He indulged in sensual pleasures.
He initially gave his maid Zǐ Guāng to the Gentleman of the Palace Sòng Yóudào.
Later, he indulged in her privately.
When he was appointed to Jì Province,
he secretly took her away.
Yóudào, in general terms, was confused and said:
"Zǐ Guāng was favored by Zhàn's father.
Zhàn's mother had left her and was about to bring her here.
The official documents have long been delayed and stopped."
Critics disapproved of both of them.
*History of the Northern Dynasties*, four.
Yù'ér.
When Yuán Shù fled to the Liáng Dynasty, he was fifteen years old.
He had not yet attained wealth and rank.
Every time he saw the clouds of Mount Sōng coming from the south,
he would invariably crane his neck and sob.
Later, he was deceived by Fán Zihú, Dù Dé, and Lǐ Zhāo
and returned north.
When he initially departed, he saw his beloved younger sister, Yù'ér,
and gave her a gold finger ring as a farewell gift.
Shù always wore it, intending to send it back.
The Liáng court expressed its intention to return it.
The imperial court knew of this.
Soon after, he was given death.
Before long, all three men died.
It was said that Shù was a vengeful spirit.
"Shàng Qī"
Chéngmǔ
Cuī Néng was by nature violent and arrogant.
He favored a concubine, Féng Shì, who was tall and beautiful.
The household called her Chéngmǔ.
Court officials such as Xíng Zǐcái and others frequently had illicit relations with her.
As a result, she exploited his power
to indulge in whatever she pleased, taking and receiving without restraint.
Thus, proper governance was not established.

Yùzhū
Dào Huī had a beloved courtesan named Chén Yùzhū.
Emperor Míng of the Sòng Dynasty sent someone to request her, but he refused.
He was coerced into surrendering her.
Huī somewhat resented the Emperor.
He instructed officials to falsely accuse him, and he was sentenced to death.
Huī was imprisoned for several nights.
His beard and hair turned completely white.
He was spared death but was stripped of his titles and fiefdom.

Měimǎn
Xiāo Jǐngxiān fell ill.
He left instructions in a memorial
to thank Emperor Shìzǔ, saying:
"Since succumbing to suffering,
His courtesans and concubines were already numerous.
Distributing the remaining ones,
Several ugly and uncouth women,
All seemed unfit for anything,
Except to be enjoyed by the bright moon.
Buddhist nun Guìzhī,
Buddhist child Yùnǚ,
Beautiful jade brought to the palace,
Their beauty and radiance are offered to the Eastern Palace."

Lù Tàixǐ
Liáng Yángkǎn was extravagant and enjoyed luxury.
He was skilled in music.
He composed two *Cǎilián Zhào Gē* (Lotus-Picking Boat Songs) himself.
They were very novel and elegant.
His concubines and courtesans attended him in rows,
Reaching the height of extravagance.
There was a *zhēng* player named Lù Tàixǐ,
Who wore a seven-inch long deer antler gourd.
The dancer Zhāng Jìngwǎn's waist was sixteen inches around.
People at the time praised her ability to dance on the palm of a hand.
There was also Sūn Jīngyù, who could bend backward to the ground,
And pick up a jade hairpin from the mat with her mouth.
The Emperor gave the singer Yù É'ér as a gift.
The Eastern Palace also bestowed the singer Qū ǒu zhī.
Both were exceptionally skilled in matching their singing to the tunes.
They were unmatched at the time.

Xuě’ér
Xuě’ér was
Lǐ Mì's beloved concubine,
skilled in singing and dancing.
Whenever she saw guests and officials,
and their writings were remarkably beautiful and pleased her,
she would have Xuě’ér adapt them to musical melodies and sing them.
Therefore, Hán Dìngcí said:
"With great virtue, one should use a silver flute to narrate beautiful words,
worthy to be sung by Xuě’ér."

Hóngfú
Lǐ Jìng visited Yáng Sù.
A courtesan, holding a red whisk, attended by his side.
She gazed at Jìng for a long time.
Jìng returned to his inn.
At night, a person in purple clothes and wearing a hat knocked on the door.
He was invited in, and he took off his clothes and hat.
It was a beautiful woman of eighteen or nineteen years old.
Jìng, surprised, questioned her.
She said:
"I am Hóngfú, a courtesan of the Yáng family.
Like dodder, I wish to entrust myself to a tall tree."
And so, they went together to Tàiyuán.

Yǎo Niáng
During the Zàichū era of Empress Wǔ,
Qiáo Zhīzhī, a secretary in the Left Bureau, had a maid named Yǎo Niáng,
whose talent and beauty were unmatched at the time.
Zhīzhī favored and cared for her,
and remained unmarried because of her.
Wǔ Yánsì heard of her and requested to see her once.
His power could not be resisted.
Once he saw her, he kept her,
with no hope of her returning.
Zhīzhī, pained and resentful, fell ill.
He wrote a poem on silk
and heavily bribed the gatekeeper to deliver it to Yǎo Niáng.
Yǎo Niáng received the poem and wept bitterly.
She tied three stanzas to her skirt
and jumped into a well to die.
Yánsì saw the poem
and sent a cruel official to falsely accuse Zhīzhī,
destroying his family.
Zhīzhī's poem said:
"The Stone Family's Golden Valley revives its music,
Ten bushels of pearls buy a beautiful woman.
In the past, you pitied her and promised her yourself,
At this time, songs and dances capture the human heart.
Your family's pavilions were never difficult to build;
You should readily lend songs and dances for people to see.
Wealth and power are not always justified;
Arrogance and extravagance forcibly intrude.
Leaving you, I ultimately cannot bear it;
In vain, I cover my sleeves and grieve for my beauty.
A hundred years of separation from a high tower,
In a single day, my beauty is exhausted for you."
The *Běnshì Shī* and the *Jiù Tángshū* are the same.
Lǐ Déyù's auspiciousness theory:
Bāo Sì and Lí Jī were both state demons bringing disaster to the country;
the Zhōu dynasty, the Jìn dynasty, Lǜzhū, and Yǎoniáng,
were all family demons,
bringing calamity to Qiáo Shí.
In the *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*, Yǎoniáng is written as Bìyù.
Xiān'é
Imperial Censor Zhāng Jí of Qīnghé's serving girl, Xiān'é, was skilled in singing and dancing, and understood writing.
She often went on missions, with É acting as the envoy's assistant.
Someone who knew the secret was about to reveal it;
Jí bowed and pleaded many times,
and in the end, it was not revealed.

Piánzhū
Yáng Guózhōng was originally a son of Zhāng Yìzhī.
At that time, Yìzhī was favored by the Empress [Wǔ Zétiān],
his favor and indulgence were unparalleled.
Every time he returned from court,
the Empress Dowager would order him to stay in the tower and have the ladder removed.
Yìzhī's mother, fearing he would have no descendants,
secretly had a female slave named Piánzhū in the tower secretly sleep with him.
Soon, she became pregnant and gave birth to Guózhōng.
Piánzhū then became the wife of Guózhōng's father, Yáng,
and her son took the surname Yáng.
Furthermore, she shared the same surname with Consort Yáng [Yáng Guìfēi],
and thus they became family members.
*The Unofficial Biography of Consort Yáng*
Sù'é
Sù'é, a courtesan of Wǔ Sānsī, possessed remarkable beauty.
Dí Rénjié requested to see her,
but she suddenly disappeared.
Within the house, a fragrance of orchids and musk was detected.
Listening closely,
he heard Sù'é say:
"I am a spirit of flowers and moonlight.
The Emperor sent me to attend to the Duke's conversations and laughter.
Duke Liáng [Dí Rénjié] is a righteous man of his time,
I dare not show myself to him."
Míngzhū
Yáng Shènjīn’s 楊慎矜 serving maid,
possessed great beauty.
She was involved in the burial of Yuán Cǎo’s 原草 blood-letting and sorcery with the diviner Shǐ Jìngsī 史敬思.
Later, she became the Eighth Concubine.
Lán Dé 闌得以 was able to gain an audience with the Emperor.
The Emperor detested her use of witchcraft,
and consequently, Shènjīn 慎矜 was punished according to the law.
*Míng Huáng Zálù* 明皇雜錄.
The serving maid Chūn Cǎo 春草 sold news of Tàizhēn’s 太真 (Yáng Guìfēi 楊貴妃) sister, of her comings and goings in the palace.
*Táng Lì* 唐曆.
Yíng Yíng 盈盈.
Dáxī Yíngyíng 達奚盈盈,
was a concubine of a nobleman during the Tiān Bǎo 天寶 era.
Her beauty and charm were unparalleled in that time.
It happened that the nobleman fell ill.
The son of a colleague, who was a imperial guard, went missing.
The search for him was very urgent.
The Emperor heard of this
and ordered a great search throughout the capital,
reaching everywhere,
but his whereabouts remained unknown.
He then asked where he had recently been.
His father said that the nobleman was ill,
and he had once gone to inquire after him.
The Emperor ordered that the nobleman's house be searched as well.
Yíngyíng 盈盈 said to the imperial guard:
"Now it is impossible to hide any longer.
"Going out won't cause any great harm."
The Qianniú (Imperial Guard) feared offending the emperor.
Yíngyíng then instructed him, saying:
"Just don't mention that you were here.
If the emperor asks where you went,
just say that the people you saw were like this,
the tents and curtains you saw were like this,
the food you ate was like this,
it was unavoidable.
There will certainly be no trouble."
After he left,
Míng Huáng was greatly angered.
He questioned him.
The guard answered as Yíngyíng had instructed.
The emperor smiled and didn't ask further.
Some days later, the Lady of the State of Guó (Guó Guó Fūrén) entered the palace.
Míng Huáng jokingly said:
"Why have you hidden your young man for so long and not brought him out?"
The Lady also just laughed.
"The Biography of Yíngyíng"
Péi Liùláng
Gēshū Hàn had a beloved concubine named Péi Liùláng.
Her appearance and demeanor were unmatched in her time.
She was skilled in singing and dancing.
*Tōng Yōu Jì* (Records Penetrating the Obscure)
Yùxiāo
Wéi Gāo, the Commissioner of the Two Chuān regions during the Táng dynasty, traveled to Jiāngxià in his youth.
They stopped at the residence of the Magistrate Jiāng.
A young man of the Jiāng family said:
"Jīng Bǎo had a young maidservant named Yùxiāo,
who was only ten years old."
He often had her attend to my elder brother Wéi.
Yùxiāo was also diligent in serving him.
Two years later, Magistrate Jiāng went to Guānzhōng to seek office.
Wéi then resided at the Shàngtóu Tuó Temple.
Jīng Bǎo sometimes sent Yùxiāo to serve and provide for him.
Yùxiāo grew older,
and thus developed feelings (for Wéi).
When Wéi later returned to visit home,
he promised Yùxiāo that he would return to fetch her in no less than five years
and no more than seven years.
He left behind a jade finger ring
and a poem for her.
When five years had passed and he still had not arrived,
Yùxiāo quietly prayed at Parrot Island.
Another year passed, and in the spring of the eighth year,
Yùxiāo sighed and said:
"It has been seven years since I parted from the young master Wéi,
he is not coming."
Thereupon, she stopped eating and died.
The Jiāng family, pitying her integrity,
placed the jade ring on her middle finger and buried her with it.
Later, Wéi was stationed in Shǔ.
Jīng Bǎo was imprisoned for some matter.
Wéi released him
He inquired about Yùxiāo's whereabouts.
Jiāng said that because Púyè had failed to keep his promise,
she had ended her life by fasting.
He then recited a poem he had left as a gift with the jade bracelet, saying:
"The yellow sparrow has brought it for several springs now,
When we parted, I left it to give to the beauty.
No letter from you comes across the Long River,
So I send my longing in dreams to Qín."
Wéi, upon hearing this, felt even more grief and lament.
He extensively commissioned scriptures and statues to repay his past affections.
Moreover, he was filled with longing and remembrance,
with no way to meet her again.
At that time, there was a hermit named Zǔ Shānrén,
who possessed the arts of shǎo Wēng,
and could cause the departed to be reunited [with the living].
He said that if the Lord would only fast for seven days,
then Yùxiāo would come on a clear night.
She expressed her gratitude, saying:
"Thanks to the power of Púyè's copying scriptures and making statues,
I shall be reborn in ten days.
Thirteen years later, I will again be your concubine,
to repay your great kindness."
As she was about to leave, she smiled and said:
"Men's fickleness has separated us in life and death."
Later, Wéi, due to his merits in Lǒngyòu, governed Shǔ.
Not failing in his duties,
he was repeatedly promoted to Chancellor of the Imperial Secretariat.
Lúqióng submitted to him.
Because it was his birthday celebration,
all the officials of the town presented rare and precious gifts as congratulations.
Only Lú, the Eighth Seat of Dōngchuān, sent a singing girl.
She had not yet reached the age of *pò guā* (maidenhood).
She was also known by the name Yùxiāo (Jade Flute).
Examining her, he realized she was truly the Yùxiāo of the Jiāng family.
On her middle finger, a fleshy ring was faintly visible,
no different from the Yùhuán (Jade Bracelet) of the farewell poem.
Wéi sighed and said:
"I now understand the distinction between existence and death,
one going and one coming.
The words of Yùxiāo
can indeed be verified."
*Yúnxī Yǒuyì*
Wáng Yǎn's palace woman included Lǐ Yùxiāo.

Xiùnú and Qīqī
Lǐ Qiāngōng Miǎn did not like common secular music.
Only his two favorite concubines, named Xiùnú and Qīqī, were intelligent
and skilled at playing the qin and zheng, and singing.
He often ordered them to perform,
and he even wrote his own qin scores.

Xuē Yáoīng
Yuán Zǎi’s beloved concubine, Xuē Yáoīng,
was skilled in poetry and books,
She excelled at singing and dancing.
Her ethereal beauty rivaled that of Wáng Zhì 王質.
Her skin exuded fragrance and her body was light.
Even the swirling waves and shimmering light,
and the dancer Zhào Fēiyàn 趙飛燕 recording pearls, could not surpass her.
Yáo Yīng's 瑤英 mother, Zhào Juān 趙娟,
was originally a beloved concubine of the Qí Prince 岐王.
Later, she married into the Xuē 薛 family,
and gave birth to Yáo Yīng, who was raised from a young age with fragrant powder,
hence her fragrant skin.
After being taken in as a concubine,
she resided in a golden silk tent,
upon a dust-repelling mattress.
The mattress came from the country of Gōulí 句驪.
It is said that it was made from the fur of a dust-repelling beast.
Its color was deep crimson,
radiant and incredibly soft.
She wore clothes of dragon silk,
each garment weighing no more than one or two liǎng (ounces),
and capable of being compressed into a handful.
Zǎi Zǎi 載 載, worried that Yáo Yīng's 瑤英 light frame would be overwhelmed by heavy clothing,
therefore sought out this fabric from foreign lands.
Only Jiǎ Zhì 賈至 and Yáng Gōngnán 楊公南 were on friendly terms with Zǎi 載,
so they often had the opportunity to witness her singing and dancing.
Zhì 賈 至 even presented her with a poem, saying:
"Do not fear the weight of the ounce-light clothes,
your smiling face opens like a peach blossom.
Compared to Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn 漢,
"He falsely constructed a wind-sheltering platform."
Gōng Nán 公南 also composed a long poem praising her beauty,
which roughly said:
"A snowy face and light eyebrows like a celestial woman,
with phoenix flutes and phoenix wings, she seems about to fly away.
Jade hairpin and verdant ornaments, her steps are dustless,
her slender waist like willow, unable to bear the spring."
Yáo Yīng 瑤英 was skilled in artful flattery,
which greatly captivated him,
causing him to neglect public affairs.
After Zǎi 載 died,
Yáo Yīng 瑤英 became the wife of a local villager.
*Dù Yáng Biān* 《杜楊編》
Xiǎo Xiǎo 小小
When Wáng Jìn 王縉 was prime minister,
he built the Bǎo Yīng Sì 寶應寺 temple for his concubine,

The *Śiva* celestial maiden figures now in the temple,
are all true portraits of Qí Gōng's 齊公 courtesan Xiǎo Xiǎo 小小 and others, painted by Hán Gàn 韓幹.

Rèn Shì 壬氏 Commands Troops
During the Dàlì 大曆 period, Cuī Níng 崔寧 replaced Dù Hóngjiàn 杜鴻漸 as the military governor of Xīchuān 西川.
Níng entered the court.
He left his younger brother Kuān to guard Chéngdū.
Yáng Zǐlín of Lúzhōu seized the opportunity and突入tūrù (suddenly charged) into Chéngdū with several thousand elite cavalry.
He occupied the city and defended it.
Kuān fought repeatedly but was overpowered.
Zǐlín's prestige was quite high.
Níng's concubine, Rèn Shì, was tall and strong, and resolute.
She took out 100,000 from her family's wealth to recruit brave warriors.
Within a few days, she obtained a thousand men.
She established ranks and appointed officers.
She personally commanded the troops.
To press Zǐlín.
Lín feared that the city's food supply would be exhausted.
He withdrew from the city and collapsed on his own.
Zǐlín had always possessed sorcery.
That evening, he caused a heavy rain.
He drew cinnabar to the courtyard.
Stepped on it and escaped.
*Jiù Táng* (Old Book of Tang) 67
Chǔ Bīn.
Lǐ Yún, the magistrate of Nánzhèng County, sought to take in a concubine in Cháng'ān,
