*Wén Qí Lù* (Record of Strange Tales)
Zhēnzhū (Pearl)
During the Bàolì era, Lǐ Yuàn
was the son of Grand Commandant Shèng.
He entered officialdom early due to his father's meritorious service.
Through repeated appointments,
he became extremely extravagant and favored many concubines.
Late in life, he obtained a young actress,
who was the most exceptional of all beauties.
He named her Zhēnzhū (真珠, Pearl),
intending to imply that Jì Lún's (季綸) Green Pearl (Lǜzhū, 綠珠) never reached this level.
As Yuàn (愿) grew old,
Zhēnzhū's (真珠) reputation became increasingly prominent.
He then consulted with his relatives and friends, saying,
"A commoner is not guilty,
but possessing jade brings guilt.
Yuàn (愿) is now old.
Yet my family possesses a treasure of a woman,
which has never been reported to the authorities.
I fear this is not proper for a subject.
If I could find a skilled writer,
like a Dēngtúzǐ (登徒子) who could describe her beauty,
I would hope to submit a memorial to present her [to the Emperor].
I would have no regrets upon my death."
His relatives then sought a memorial from Hàngōng (漢公),
but Hàngōng (漢公) declined, saying he was unable to write it.
So they told Yú Qīng (虞卿),
and Yú Qīng (虞卿) wanted to draft it himself,
saying,
"I must see her once,
so her appearance is etched in my mind,
then I can compose the writing."
Yuàn (愿) agreed.
Yú Qīng, upon seeing this courtesan once,
was dazed and lost himself,
realizing she was unattainable.
He then spoke of it to Niú Sēngrú.
Sēngrú was at that time holding the reins of state.
He said,
"Whatever do you desire?
I can obtain it for you;
why must it even be reported to the emperor?"
Yú Qīng said,
"My desire is already decided.
If Your Excellency were to simply seize her,
I fear it would not be to your liking.
But if you were to obtain her through a plan,
you would certainly succeed."
He then recommended Hàn Gōng as a messenger,
saying,
"This man can wag his three-inch tongue
and move a man's very heart."
Sēngrú agreed with him.
Hàn Gōng then went to see Yuàn and said,
"I have heard that the Minister of Public Works wishes to present a courtesan as tribute;
is there truly such a thing?"
Yuàn said,
"Yes."
Hàn Gōng said,
"I am deeply concerned for the Minister of Public Works."
Yuàn was surprised and said,
"How could it be dangerous?"
Hàn Gōng 漢公 said:
"Now, the current emperor is at the height of his youth and strength,
and in the inner palace, there are thousands of women as beautiful as Xī Shī 西施.
The Sīkōng 司空 is now giving them real pearls,
which is no different than throwing a grain of rice into a great granary.
If Zhēnzhū 真珠 receives the emperor's favor,
and the emperor changes his mind,
her influence will overshadow the six palaces.
She will certainly blame the Sīkōng 司空 for keeping her to himself for so long,
and for not presenting her all these years.
Yesterday, upon reflection,
I realized that the Sīkōng 司空 is in danger."
Yuàn 愿 said, greatly startled:
"What should be done?"
Hàn Gōng 漢公 said:
"Generally speaking, exceptionally beautiful women
are certain to bring disaster to people.
Whether Zhēnzhū 真珠 is presented or not,
I fear that she will eventually bring disaster to the Sīkōng 司空.
Furthermore, I have secretly heard that the Sīkōng 司空 has wanted to present this courtesan for a long time.
If he stops suddenly,
people will surely say that the Sīkōng 司空 is infatuated and unable to let her go.
For the sake of the Sīkōng 司空,
it would be better to give her to someone else."
Yuàn 愿 said:
"Who could she be given to?"
Hàn Gōng 漢公 said:
"Niú Xiàng has been seeking a beautiful woman for a long time.
Now, Sīkōng is merely seeking a large commandery.
He hopes to turn the will of Heaven.
Why not give her to Niú Xiàng?
Niú Xiàng gets the courtesan,
and Sīkōng gets the commandery.
Wouldn't that be wonderful?"
Yuàn was greatly pleased,
and so he used the pearls to return to Sēngrú.
Hàn Gōng then became a frequent guest,
using the pearls as instruments for pleasure.
Although dukes, ministers, and envoys from all directions
urgently desired to see him once but could never manage it,
therefore, the capital called Yú Qīng the "prime minister's matchmaker,"
which originated from this.

Huángfǔ Sōng Niú Qí,

Resenting that Gōng did not recommend him,
he wrote a slanderous poem saying:
"At night I enter the Zhēnzhū Chamber,

Zhēnzhū was the name of Gōng's concubine.
*Zhi Yan*
Zhēnzhū was acquired when he was garrisoned in Xiāngyáng.
She had an extraordinary appearance,
and her singing and dancing were

Duke Qízhāng took in a courtesan, saying:

Lú Zhào arrived at Qízhāng's place.
Appreciating her writing,
he was invited to the inner chamber.
It happened that Zhēnzhū was washing her hair.
She was holding her hair in her hands,

The Chancellor said:

Zhào said:

*Yínchuāng Xùlù* (A Record from the Singing Window)
*Jiàngtáo* and *Liǔzhī*
Hán Tuìzhī's two concubines,
one named *Jiàngtáo*,
the other named *Liǔzhī*.
Tuìzhī was sent to Shāndōng.
There is a poem that says:
"The east wind stirs, about to depart from Cháng'ān,
mid-spring in the border city is especially cold.
I do not see garden flowers nor alley willows,
only the round moon at the horse's head."
Later, *Liǔzhī* went over the garden wall and fled.
She had a poem that said:
"Since parting, the willow trees by the steps,
Sway in the chaotic spring wind, longing to fly away.

*Yǔ Lín*
Guān Xìnxìn
Lè Tiān has a poem "Hé Yànzi Lóu Shī" (Responding to the Swallow Tower Poem),
the preface to which says:
"The Director Zhāng of Xú Prefecture also had a beloved courtesan, Xìnxìn,
skilled in singing and dancing,
and of refined and graceful demeanor.
When I was a proofreader, I traveled between the Huái and Sì rivers.
Director Zhāng held a banquet for me,
and, as the wine flowed, he presented Xìnxìn to add to the merriment.
Consequently, I gifted her a poem, with the concluding lines:
'Her drunken allure is unmatched,
Like a peony flower swaying in the breeze.'
After that single joyful encounter,
I never learned of her again."
"Now a full cycle of twelve years has passed.
Yesterday, the Secretary of Merit Zhang Zhòngsù, painted a picture and visited me,
where he recited three "Yànzi Lóu Shī" poems,
the words were graceful and beautiful.
When asked about their origin,
he revealed they were written by Xìnxìn,
who was working on the painting.
I have learned that Wǔníng Commandery had, for years, known the whole story of Xìnxìn.
It is said that after Zhāng Shàngshū (張尚書) had died,
in Péngchéng (彭城) there was an old house of the Zhāng (張) family,
in which there was a small building named Yànzi (燕子),
where Xìxì (盻盻), cherishing her old love, did not marry.
She lived in this building for more than ten years,
and is still there to this day.
Xìxì's (盻盻) poem says:
"Upstairs, a flickering lamp keeps company with the morning frost,
the lonely sleeper rises from the Héhuān (合歡) bed.
How much longing is there in one night of mutual love?
The corners of the earth and the edge of the sky are not far enough."
Another poem says:
"On the Běimáng (北邙) hills, pines and cypresses lock in melancholy mist,
the Yànzi (燕子) Tower's resident thinks quietly.
Since the burial of sword and shoes, the songs and dust have scattered,
the fragrance of red sleeves has faded for ten years."
Another poem says:
"Just now I saw the wild geese returning to Yuèyáng (岳陽),
and again I see the dark birds approaching the spring festival.
I have no mood for jade zithers or jade flutes,
letting the spiderwebs be, letting the dust be."
I have always loved her new works,
so I harmonized with them, saying:
"The window is full of bright moonlight, the curtain is full of frost,
the quilt is cold, the lamp is dying, I dust the bed before lying down.
In the Yànzi (燕子) Tower on a cold moonlit night,
autumn comes only for one person's increased longing.
The color of the ornamented belt and silk dress is like smoke,
Several times I wanted to rise up, but then desisted.
Since I no longer dance the "Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Dress" song,
it has been folded in an empty chest for twelve years."
Also, "This spring, a visitor returned from Luòyáng,
and unexpectedly came to the Shàngshū's (Minister's) grave.
Hearing it said that white poplars could be used as pillars,
how could red powder not turn to ash?"
He also presented a four-line poem:
"I didn't borrow gold to buy beautiful eyebrows,
but selected four or five branches like flowers.
Teaching song and dance exhausted my heart and strength,
but once his body departed, I did not follow."
Later, Zhòng Sù showed my poem to Xì Xì,
who repeatedly read it,
and wept, saying:
"Since my lord passed away,
it's not that I couldn't die,
but I feared that after a hundred years, people would say my lord valued beauty too much,
having a concubine who died for him,
which would stain my lord's pure reputation,
so I selfishly continued to live."
Thereupon, she replied to Bái Gōng's poem, saying:
"Guarding the empty tower alone, I gather my hateful brows,
my form like a peony branch after spring.
The aide does not understand my deep intention,
and wonders why I do not follow him to the Yellow Springs."
After Xì Xì received the poem,
she was dejected for ten days,
He died without eating.
He only chanted:
"Children do not recognize things that soar to the heavens,
Foolishly using blue mud to sully the white fur brush."
*Cháng Qìng Jí*
In Xúzhōu, the Swallow Tower was directly behind the prefectural residence.
It was built by Zhāng Jiànfēng, the Tang dynasty military commissioner, for his concubine, Xì Xì.
Chén Yànshēng once left a poem:
"The Minister's desolate grave, a lonely rabbit wanders.
The concubine still dwells in the Water West Tower.
The wind is clear, the jade mat makes the singing pillow feel lazy.
The moon is beautiful, the pearl curtain is too lazy to be hooked up.
Waking from a cold dream, the vast ocean seems immense.
After chanting new sorrows, it is the autumn of purple orchids.
Lètiān's talent resembles the deep spring rain.
Sending off the remaining flowers in one evening's rest."
*Xī Qīng Shīhuà*
Fán Sù and Xiǎo Mán:
Bái Lètiān had two concubines.

He once had a poem that said:

Willow Xiǎo Mán's waist."
After the two concubines grew old,
he had another poem that said:

Later, the two concubines each departed.
There's a poem that says:

Chūn Cǎo (Spring Grass)
Liú Mèngdé's collection has a poem presented to Little Fán:

Jǐn Sè (Brocade Zither)
Lǐ Shāngyǐn has the poem *Jǐn Sè*,

*Gòng Fù Shī Huà* (Gòng Fù's Discussions of Poetry)
The sound of the *jǐn sè*,
evokes feelings of resentment and harmonious purity.
Formerly, a serving girl of Línghú Chǔ could play these four lines.
The four lines in the poem
describe these four tunes.
Zhāng Zǐhòu once questioned this poem,

Shěn Zhēnzhēn (沈真真)
Tài Cháng Bóshì Zhèng Huángǔ (太常博士鄭還古) resided in the Eastern Capital (Dōng Dū).
He lived in the same alley as General Liǔ (柳).
Huángǔ (還古) was about to be transferred to the Western Capital (Xī Dū).
Liǔ (柳) lavishly set up a banquet to bid him farewell.
He brought out all his family's courtesans.
They sang, danced, and offered wine as the cups were passed around.
One of the three concubines was extraordinarily beautiful and charming.
Zhèng (鄭) secretly peeked at her.
He showed a deep affection.
Liǔ (柳) said to Zhèng (鄭):
"This is Shěn Zhēnzhēn (沈真真).
She was originally from a good family.
She has a fondness for literature.
Please compose a poem to express your feelings.
Once the Doctor (Bóshì) receives his appointment,
I will send her as a congratulatory gift."
Huángǔ (還古) composed a poem, saying:
"A celestial being emerges from the boudoir.
Her clear voice surpasses pipes and strings.
Her words are light like the 'White Ramie Song' (Bái Zhù Qǔ),
Her song lifts up the 'White Cloud Ode' (Bái Yún Piān).
Since Péi Xiù (裴秀) is not yet born,
Why not beg from Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄)?
I cannot bear the Jīngǔ (金谷) stream,
to flow across the front of the suicide tower."
Liǔ Lǎn read the poem and was overjoyed.
He had Zhēnzhēn bow and thank him.
He returned to Gǔ and headed to the capital.
Soon after, he was appointed Magistrate of Yī Quē.
He contracted a serious illness.
He urgently sent a letter to Liǔ.
Liǔ immediately sent Zhēnzhēn to the capital.
He welcomed Zhèng and requested to see him.
Zhēnzhēn adorned herself and bowed respectfully.
Gǔ rose and stepped forward,
suddenly grasped Zhēnzhēn's hand,
sighed deeply, and then died.
*Lì Qíng Jí* ("Collection of Beautiful Sentiments")
Liǔ Chùnyīng
Yú Mèiniáng was a talented woman,
married to a man surnamed Zhōu.
After her husband died, she remained chaste and guarded herself.
Lù Xīshēng was serving as a *zhèng láng* (official rank).
Hearing of her beautiful appearance and skill in calligraphy,
and her unparalleled cleverness,
he sent a well-spoken messenger to act as a matchmaker to persuade her.
Mèiniáng said,
"If Master Lù wishes for me to serve him with comb and towel [as his wife],
he must vow not to take concubines or female slaves.
Then I will become a new bride of the Lù family."
Xīshēng agreed to it.
Two years after the marriage,
Splitting paper and grinding ink,
singing and harmonizing in turns.
Mèi Niáng could also prepare colorful sliced raw fish,
her skill was unparalleled.
Soon after, Xī Shēng acquired a famous courtesan named Liǔ Chùn Yīng.
Mèi Niáng resented this.
She ordered her to enter the household and live with them.
Xī Shēng thought this was genuine.
After they lived together,
there were no other discussions.
When Xī Shēng went elsewhere,
she immediately summoned Chùn Yīng,
locked her in a room, and personally killed her with a knife.
She minced her flesh,
and placed it in two large boxes,
sealing them with a label that read:
"Returning items to the villa."
The gatekeeper found it strange,
and sent it to the Jingzhao Prefecture prison.
Mèi Niáng was then sentenced to the most severe punishment.
Dù Qiū Niáng.
Lǐ Qí's rebellion involved a concubine, Dù Qiū Niáng.
She was confiscated into the palace and later released.
Dù Mù was moved by this and wrote a poem, which said:
"Peppercorn walls hung with silk curtains,
dressing cases coiled with jade dragons.
The moon rises over the white jade gate,
The laurel's shadow floats, mottled and uneven.
On the golden steps, the jade dew is heavy,
Leisurely, I hold the purple flute and blow.
The swallow served as the matchmaker and obtained a prince,
The lady herself held the swaddling clothes.
A tiger charm protects the pearly net swaddling,
A rhinoceros horn paperweight settles the curtain on the golden tray."
*Guó Shǐ Bǔ* (Supplement to the National History)
Qín Kè,
Liǔ Yíchéng's beloved concubine,
Skilled in playing the qin and se,
Yíchéng requested retirement, and Qín Kè was released,
Married Gù Kuàng,
Who composed a song for her.
*Lì Qíng Jí* (Collection of Beautiful Sentiments)
Què Yào
The surveillance commissioner Lǐ Gēng's slave girl was named Què Yào,
With unsurpassed beauty,
Skilled in rhetoric,
Lǐ had four sons,
The eldest was named Yánxī,
The next Yánfàn, Yánzuò, Yányòu,
Referred to as the Eldest, Second, Third, and Fifth Sons,
All desired to seduce her but could not.
Once, on a Qingming night,
The Eldest Son encountered her in the shadow of a cherry blossom tree,
Thereupon she took it and sought a mate.
But she wanted to take mats and cushions and give them to them,
deceiving them and saying:
"You may wait at the southeast corner of the hall."
Then she met the second son,
and directed him, saying:
"You may wait for each other at the northeast corner of the hall."
Then she met the third son,
and instructed him, saying:
"You may wait for each other at the southwest corner of the hall."
Then she met the fifth son, who grasped her hand tightly and wouldn't let go, and she said:
"You may wait for each other at the northwest corner of the hall."
The four sons, each holding the mats and cushions they had been given,
each went to a corner.
Though they were surprised, they dared not speak out.
Soon, she wanted to light a torch and fling open the door,
illuminating them and saying:
"You poor wretches,
how dare you seek lodging here!"
The four sons each abandoned what they carried,
covered their faces, and fled.
From then on, they dared not be disrespectful.
*Sānshuǐ Xiǎodú*
Fēi Yān
Lín Huái Wǔ Gōngyè served as the registrar of Hénán Prefecture during the Xiántōng era.
His military advisor's beloved concubine, named Fēi Yān,
had a delicate and beautiful appearance,
Ruo could not be surpassed in fine silk garments,
skilled in Qin music,
fond of literary writing,
Gōngyè greatly favored her.
Her neighbor, the son of the Zhào family, named Xiàng,
was handsome and refined with literary talent,
barely twenty years old.
Suddenly one day, he glimpsed Fēiyān through a crack in the south wall,
and his spirit and energy were completely lost.
He lost his appetite and forgot to sleep.
He then heavily bribed Gōngyè's gatekeeper,
and told him his feelings.
The gatekeeper's wife told Fēiyān all about it,
but she only smiled and gazed intently without replying.
The old woman of the gate told Xiàng everything.
Xiàng's heart went wild and unrestrained,
not knowing what to do.
So he took a Xuē Tāo note and wrote a quatrain on it, saying:
"Once I saw her captivating beauty,
my worldly heart could only guess.
I won't follow Xiāo Shǐ away,
I plan to learn from Ā Lán to come."
He secretly sealed what he had written,
and asked the old woman of the gate to deliver it to Fēiyān.
After reading it, Yān sighed for a long time,
and said to the old woman:
"I also once glimpsed Zhao láng's great talent and handsome appearance.
My life is unfortunate,
She could not accept this,
for she despised the crude and boorish martial scholar,
and he was not a suitable match for her."
Thereupon, she composed a reply on a golden phoenix stationery, saying:
"Green sorrowful eyebrows cannot contain themselves,
only green resentment lies in this new poem.
My lover's heart must be like the zither's heart, full of grievances,
to whom can I confide these silent spring sorrows?"
She sealed it and gave it to the gatekeeper woman,
instructing her to give it to Xiàng.
Xiàng opened the seal and recited the poem several times,
clapping his hands with joy and saying:
"My affair is going to succeed!"
Later, when Gōngyè was on duty,
they indulged in deep affection,
and this went on for a year.
Later, she was denounced by a maidservant,
and Gōngyè was whipped to death.

Sù'é.
Wéi Xúnměi passed the imperial examination during the Kaicheng era,
and was appointed by the Deng capital as an assistant official.
He took his beloved Sù'é with him.
Luó Shàowēi heard of her beauty and elegance,
and asked for her.
Xúnměi dared not refuse,
so he presented her to him.
Sù É, her surname was Cuī,
a good family's daughter from Dàliáng.
She was skilled at humorous writing,
and composed a poem with tears:
"I am confined to a quiet room, while you are on a diverging road;
my heart and your regret are both longing.
If my spirit could meet with a sorceress,

Xún Měi refused to accept her,
and he secretly crossed the river at night, staying overnight in a temple.
He sighed deeply, unable to sleep, saying:
"Where can a person report injustice?"
There was a traveling monk in the temple who asked about the injustice.
Xún Měi told him everything,
and the monk suddenly left.
Around the third watch, he suddenly threw a leather bag,

At daybreak, Xún Měi asked the monks in the temple
and they said that the monk had been striking the bell in the temple
diligently for more than thirty years,
and they did not know where he had gone.
Xún Měi then fled to another place.
*Idle Talks Under the Lamp*
Jiě Chóu
Pān Kàng and his younger brother Qiào both served Shǔ Wáng Jiàn, managing important affairs,
known as the Great Pivot and Small Pivot.
Kàng favored his beautiful concubine Jiě Chóu,
Suì fēng yàng chéng jí.
Jiěchóu's surname was Zhào,

She possessed considerable beauty.
She was skilled at composing new melodies and writing short poems.
Jiàn Zhì came to Kàng's residence.
Upon seeing her, he said,

He intended to take her.
Kàng said,

His younger brother Qiào said,

Kàng said,

*Wàishǐ Táojī*
Dǎ Fèng.
Dù Dàzhōng rose from the ranks to become a general.
He empathized with objects.
The Westerners called him Dù Dàchóng.
Even if his wife had faults,
he would publicly cane her.
He had a beloved concubine who possessed both talent and beauty.
Dàzhōng's memorials were all written by her.
One day, Dà Zhōng 大中 was resting.

Dà Zhōng 大中 awoke and saw it.

*Jīn Shì Táng Shǒu Lù*《今是堂手錄》
Lián Huā 蓮花
Chén Táo 陳陶, a recluse of the Southern Táng 南唐 Dynasty, lived in the Western Mountains.
His conduct and behavior were pure and clean.
At that time, Yán Zhuàn 嚴譔, the governor of Yùzhāng 豫章, wanted to disturb him.
He sent his concubine, Lián Huā 蓮花, there frequently.
Táo 陶 paid her no attention.
The concubine then presented a poem requesting to leave, saying:
"Lián Huā 蓮花 is my name, jade is my cheek,

Táo 陶 replied:
"Recently, my poetic thoughts are clear as water,
As I grow old, my amorous feelings are as thin as clouds.

*Lì Qíng Jí* 《麗情集》
Later people transferred this event to Chén Túnán 陳圖南, which is incorrect.
Zhào Yángtái.
Dòu Tāo, zì Liánbō,
his wife, Sū Shì, named Huì,
zì Ruòlán,
was the third daughter of Dào Zhì, the magistrate of Chénliú and originally from Wǔgōng.
She married at sixteen.
Tāo served as the governor of Qínzhōu under Fú Jiān.
He was demoted and exiled to Dūnhuáng for violating an imperial decree.
Later, he was appointed General of Annam and stationed in Xiāngyáng
to defend against the Jìn dynasty.
Initially, Tāo had a favored concubine, Zhào Yángtái,
whose singing and dancing were unmatched.
Tāo housed her in a separate residence.
Sū Shì, upon learning of this,
harshly abused and humiliated her.
Tāo deeply resented this.
Yángtái, furthermore, took every opportunity to find fault with and denigrate Sū,
which further angered Tāo.
Sū Shì was twenty-one years old at the time.
When Tāo was about to be stationed in Xiāngyáng,
Sū Shì was indignant
and refused to accompany him.
Tāo then took Yángtái with him to his post,
cutting off all communication with Sū.
Sū Shì, filled with regret and self-pity,
wove a brocade palindrome of five colors,
eight inches in length and width,
totaling more than eight hundred and forty characters,
vertically, horizontally, forward, and backward, all forming complete sentences and paragraphs.
The text's dots and strokes are without omission,
and it is named the *Xuánjī Tú* (璇璣圖, Armillary Sphere Diagram).
However, readers cannot fully understand it.
Madame Sū (蘇氏) smiled and said to people,
"Wandering and circling,
it forms its own composition;
if not my fair lady,
none can decipher it."
Thereupon, she sent a servant to carry it to Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Tāo (滔) examined the brocade characters,
and was moved by its exquisite wonder.
Consequently, he sent a message to Yángtái (陽臺) Pass,
and with elaborate carriage and retinue, respectfully invited Madame Sū (蘇氏) to return to Hànnán (漢南).
Their affection and favor grew ever stronger.
*Táng Wǔ Hòu Jì* (唐武后紀, Records of Empress Wǔ of the Tang Dynasty)
and the *Jìn Shū* (晉書, Book of Jin) differ slightly.
Imitating "Four Sorrows"
Lǐ Féngjí (李逢吉) was stubborn, obstinate, and suspicious.
He enjoyed endangering people.
Liú Yǔxī (劉禹錫) had a very beautiful courtesan.
Lǐ (李) plotted secretly,
arranging a meeting to seize her.
Liú (劉) returned home, distraught, sighing, and lamenting,
knowing there was nothing he could do.
Thus, he composed four poems in resentment,
This is written to imitate the "Four Sorrows":
"The jade hairpin can be rejoined, but the two are without fate;
the fish is in the deep pool, the crane is in the sky.
The complacent purple Luan bird should stop dancing before the mirror;
the talking green bird should cease carrying letters.
Once the golden basin is overturned, it's hard to gather the water;
the jade zither is thrown away for good, and the strings are not replaced.
If you pass by the Xiāo Wú 𧃲蕪 Mountain,
from afar, scatter red tears upon the poor springs.
Where does the Luan bird, having left its old companion, now reside?
The phoenix has found a new nest and is content.
Rouge still remains, fragrance faint;
the azure clouds are newly broken, news is heavy and sunken.
Knowing full well it's like soiling jade by throwing it into mud,
still, I persevered in scheming for the money to buy a smile.
From now on, the man on the mountain resembles stone,
the shape of a husband, deep with tear stains.
I searched and looked everywhere for places we used to visit together,
though alive, it is like being separated by death.
The flowers before the Mǎi Xiào Lóu 買笑樓 (Smile-Buying Pavilion) are already old,

Clouds hide Wū Xiá 巫峽 (Witches Gorge), her voice and appearance are cut off;
the road is separated by the Star Bridge, it's hard to pass back and forth.
Don't say that the poem is completed without tears dripping;
even emptying the Eastern Sea, it must be dried up.
The Three Mountains are unseen, the sea is deep and vast,
how could there be immortal traces that can still be found?
When the green bird left, the cloud road was cut off;
Héng'é returned, deeply into the Moon Palace.
Thinking of spring from afar through the gauze window,
Who pities the solitary吟(yín) in the night with the swaying book?
I imagine that the heavenly mirror from last night
Must have shone only on the hearts of two people."

Idle talk under the moon believes this to be about the wife of Huáng Sǔn,

One last poem without an ending.
After Sǔn, he met an old man,

*Xiāngyáng Guīqiè* (The Returned Concubine of Xiangyang)
Cuī Jiāo, a Xiùcai (successful candidate in the imperial examination),
lived in Hànshàng.
He accumulated literary talent but his possessions were completely exhausted.
Soon after,
he had an affair with his aunt's maid.
He often acted like Ruan Xian.
The maid was beautiful
and possessed the ability to play music.
She was the most beautiful in southern Hán.
Initially poor,
he sold the maid to a military commander.
The commander loved her,
considering her unparalleled.
Wu Shuang,
Tài Bǎo of Xuē loved a concubine,
whose portrait is still viewed today.
He paid 400,000 coins for her,
and his favor and affection for her deepened.
Jiāo Sī, longing for her without end,
even boldly went to Tài Bǎo's mansion,
hoping to see her just once.
Her maid took advantage of the Hánshí Festival to tend to the grave.
Jiāo stood at the edge of the suburb under the shade of a willow tree,
weeping continuously on horseback,
vowing like mountains and rivers,
and Cuī Shēng gifted him a poem, saying:
"Noble sons and grandsons chase after the dust,
Green Pearl sheds tears, dripping onto the silk.
Once you enter the gates of a noble house, it's as deep as the sea,
From then on, Xiāo Láng is just a stranger."
Someone who disliked Jiāo wrote his poem on a seat.
The commander saw it,
and ordered Cuī Shēng to be summoned.
Those around him were unable to understand what this meant.
Jiāo was deeply worried, feeling there was nowhere to hide.
When he saw Jiāo,
he shook his hand and said:
"'Once you enter the gates of a noble house, it's as deep as the sea,
From then on, Xiāo Láng is just a stranger,'
is indeed your writing.
Four hundred thousand is a small sum,
why did you begrudge showing me the poem earlier?"
Thereupon, he ordered the woman to return together.
As for the curtains, canopies, dressing cases, and jewelry boxes,
he had them all embellished and adorned,
creating a small mountain of treasures.
Initially, a guest came from Línglíng,
calling himself Róng Yù.
The local governor had a skilled singer at his banquet.
Duke Xiāngyáng immediately ordered her to be summoned.
How could Governor Róng dare to disobey the order?
She arrived more than a month later.
When she arrived and was asked to sing, it turned out to be one of Governor Róng’s own poems,
which said:
"With jeweled hairpins, fragrant eyebrows, and a jade-green skirt,
she finishes dressing, hides her tears, and is about to float away like a cloud.
Earnestly try to capture the heart of King Xiāng,
do not let her dream of her former lord at Yángtái."
The Duke said,
"If a man cannot establish merit and achieve accomplishments,
to be praised by later generations,
how can he seize another man's beloved concubine for his own amusement?"
Judging from this,
he should truly hide himself away in a desolate, uninhabited place.
So, he generously presented her with silks and fabrics for her journey,
and sent a letter of apology to the governor of Línglíng.
In the past, Wáng Dūn used female entertainers to win over his soldiers,
and Yáng Sù returned Xú Déyán’s wife, showing that one should not be greedy for wealth,
and not stingy with beauty.
At that time, people used this as refined conversation.
Can Xiāngyáng Gōng be considered an outstanding hero?
From *Yúnxī Yǒuyì*
In Gāolì (Korea), on the banks of the river, in Pōjiāng (Slope River), there lived a scholar whose name has been forgotten.
There was a beautiful woman who was very poor.
She sought a short composition from him to sell in the Jiāogǔang region.
He traveled extensively, seeking ten thousand [coins],
enough to support five years of food.
He cautioned the woman, saying:
"If I do not return in five years,
you are free to remarry."
After the scholar left, he did not return for five years.
The woman was then taken in by a former prefect.
She was at the foot of Pōjiāng in Gāolì.
The following year, the scholar returned,
having already lost track of the woman's whereabouts.
After searching and discovering her location,
he composed a poem seeking an intermediary,
and sent it, the poem saying:
"Dark clouds descend heavily on Yángtái,
causing King Xiāng to linger and never return.
Five years passed without return, only tears remained,
My heart tied in a knot, never opened.
Fine vines naturally cling to fragrant trees,
But spilled water cannot be returned to the old cup.
I am sad at the house at the foot of Pōjiāng in Gāolì;
Spring will never come down from the mountains again."
When the regional inspector saw the poem,
he then provided 100,000 *qián* and travel expenses,
and immediately sent the scholar back.
From *Lú Shì Zá Shuō* (Miscellaneous Sayings of Mr. Lú)
New Voice
Zhāng Gǔ served as an assistant to Liú Cóngjiàn.
Cóngjiàn took a daughter of Lǐ Yán from Hándān as a personal attendant,
and she was called New Voice.
When Cóngjiàn was secretly planning to peep and threaten New Voice,
Gǔ said to him:
"Initially, the Son of Heaven considered Cóngjiàn as a *jiédù* (military commissioner) not because
he had merit in fighting battles in the fields and attacking cities,
but simply because his father brought the twelve prefectures of Qí back to the Son of Heaven.
In the interval of abandoning one and going to another, he was just unable to seize his inheritance.
Ever since the Zé-Lù region existed,
I have not heard of them offering a single thread or a single hoof as longevity gifts to the Son of Heaven.
All your attendants are scoundrels.
During the Zhāng Wǔ reign, several towns were overturned.
Even with heroic talent and outstanding abilities, they were still unable to secure them.
The Son of Heaven favored Cóngjiàn, promoting him from among young children.
If he does not act according to the law,
it is also fitting that he ends unlawfully.
You should take your clan and flee west.
A great man should not be concerned about the favor of a single meal,
and use the flesh and blood to feed the strong soldiers."
After speaking, he wept sadly.
Gǔ hesitated for three months,
Fearing to speak out,
the consequences and misfortune will follow.

Tíng Tíng, the favored concubine of Yuán, the Prince of Lújiāng,

When Lǐ Shè arrived in Yángzhōu,
he visited various temples.
He passed a woman
who bowed and wept, claiming to be Sòng Xióng.
Sòng Xióng was
formerly the beloved concubine of the gentleman Liú from Wúxīng.
The Liú was utterly white-haired.

so he presented her with a poem, saying:
"I often recall when Yún Xiān was young,
with beautiful face and green silk tied on her head.
At that time, I startledly awoke from a dream of Gāo Táng,
only now Sòng Yù knows."
He also said:
"At the Héngyáng night banquet, at the magistrate's feast,
a 'flower that understands speech' is right before my eyes.

Master Lǐ sighed and said:
"To not see Háo Shǒu with his disheveled hair,

Fàn Yuánshí,

Sū Dōngpō had concubines named Cháoyún and Liú Huā.

Consider the line, "The floating flowers and wandering pistils have all gone,"

Cuì Qiáo, a servant of Hóng nèihàn

She inscribed her paintings with the words:

Yīngyīng and Yànyàn
Fàn Shíláng of Qiántáng had two daughters who both became concubines of a wealthy man named Lù in Yúnjiān.
The elder was named Yīngyīng,
who was favored but died young.

and was treated like the other concubines.
Lù became ill and impoverished,
so he sold the house where he lived and the tomb where he planned to be buried.
The other concubines scattered,
but Yàn alone could not bear to leave.

Alas,

How could Yàn be considered less virtuous than Ràng!

Zāng Huò
In the *Biography of Sīmǎ* in the Former Han Dynasty, *zāng huò* refers to male and female slaves.

to scold a male slave is *zāng*,
and to scold a female slave is *huò*."
Also, the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says of being employed:

is the northern suburb of Yan.

Zhāng Yì said:

and the son of a woman who marries a male slave is called *huò*."
The *Fēng Sú Tōng* says:

huò zhě táo wáng,

Initially, the page boy of the Marquis of Jin, Tóu Xū, was a keeper of treasures.

Virtuous Conduct.
Lǐ Shàn, courtesy name Cìsūn,
was originally a servant of Lǐ Yuán.
During the Jianwǔ period, the Yuán family suffered successive epidemics, and all died,
leaving only the orphaned son Xù, newly born.
After several weeks, the various slaves and婢 (bì) wanted to kill Jì and divide the property.
Shàn, grieved, could not stop them.
He carried Xù and fled to the border of Xiáqiū County,
personally caring for him,
producing milk for him to drink,
taking the dry bedding for himself and giving the wet to the infant.
Even in his infancy,
he treated him as a senior lord,
kneeling and asking permission before doing anything.
The neighborhood was touched by this.
When Xù was ten years old,
Shàn then returned with him to the old family estate in the county,
reported the slaves and婢 (bì) to the officials,
and had them all arrested and killed.
Zhōnglí Yì submitted a memorial detailing the situation.
Emperor Shìzǔ issued an edict appointing both Shàn and Xù
as Attendants to the Crown Prince.
Later, he became the Grand Administrator of Rìnán.
Passing by Yuán's tomb on the road,
he personally cleared weeds and sprinkled the road.
He personally took charge of cooking and preparing offerings for sacrifices.
He bowed and bid farewell, weeping as he left.

Chén Guó Gōngsūn Zhìjié, the Grand Artisan of the Directorate of Imperial Buildings, had a servant named Dì Yú.
At the age of seventeen,
he was intelligent and clever in nature,
and his appearance was dignified and proper.
He was skilled in calligraphy.
Zhìjié made him a clerk in the Household Affairs Office.
He ordered Dì Yú to go home to fetch supplies.
Thereupon, taking advantage of the carriages and horses, he fled.
He arrived in Dānyáng,
claiming his surname was Wáng and his given name was Bīn,
styled Wéngāo.
He then remained there, becoming a clerk in various offices.
Zhìjié was appointed Inspector of Yángzhōu.
The county selected young men from official families, all of whom were placed under Bīn.
Thus, he employed him.
Bīn asked to dismiss those around him,
kowtowed, and wept, saying,
"Bīn is none other than your servant, Dì Yú."
Bīn later became the Grand Administrator of Cāngwú.

Qiú bài

Access to his wife's quarters:
Liáng Jì loved the supervising slave Qín Gōng.
He was appointed as the magistrate of Tàicāng,
and allowed to enter and exit his wife's quarters.
Every time he saw her, he dismissed the attendants to discuss matters,
and as a result, he had an affair with her.
He enjoyed favor both inside and outside the household,
and even governors and officials with salaries of two thousand dan visited and paid their respects to him.
Sūn Fèn, a man of Fúfēng, lived in wealth.
Jì borrowed fifty million coins from him.
Fèn gave him thirty million coins.
Jì was greatly angered,
and thus informed the commanderies and counties,
falsely accusing Fèn's mother of being a storehouse maid,
claiming she stole ten *hú* of white pearls,
and one thousand *jīn* of purple-ground gold,
using this as a pretext for rebellion, and consequently arrested and interrogated her.
Fèn's brothers died in prison,
and all their loaned wealth was confiscated.

When I read the "Biography of the Xiongnu" in the *Hàn Shū* (Book of Han),

From "Shì Shuō Xīn Yǔ":
The envoy from Sea Mountain.
Tao Kan had over a thousand household servants,
often acquiring barbarian slaves.
He disliked speaking and
often sat silently.
One day Kan went out to the suburbs,
and the slave followed, holding a whip.
A foreign monk saw him and, surprised, bowed and said,
"This is the envoy from Sea Mountain,"
and then shed tears.
Kan found it strange.
By night, he had disappeared.
Helping labor:
Tao Kan was serving as magistrate of Pengze.
He did not want to burden his family.
He sent a laborer along with a letter to his son, which said:
"Your expenses, morning and evening,
are difficult to cover on your own.
Now I am sending this laborer to help you with the work of firewood and water.
This is also the son of a human being, you should treat him kindly."
Fond of escaping:
Zhāng Cúnshàn's needles:
Someone had a slave who was prone to running away.
When the slave was staying put, Zhāng Cúnshàn would insert needles to shrink the slave's feet.
When he wanted the slave to work, he would remove the needles.
*Dùnhuáng Shílù* (Veritable Records of Dunhuang)
Diǎn Qín:
Wáng Yuánjǐng of the Northern Qi Dynasty was a *shàngshū* (high-ranking official).
Although he was by nature scholarly and easygoing, he was quick-witted in all matters.
He had a slave named Diǎn Qín.
Once, he got up in the morning and ordered him to find food,
calling it "breaking the fast" (*jiězhāi*).
The slave said:
"Sir, you are not observing a fast,
why do you always say 'breaking the fast'?"
Yuánjǐng slowly said to the slave:
"If I am not observing a fast,
I cannot say 'breaking the fast.'
You are named Diǎn Qín (典琴, lit. "to pawn a *qín*"),
where is there a *qín* that you can pawn?"
*Qǐ Yán Lù* (Record of Opening Smiles)
Admiring the master's erudition:
Xiāo Yǐngshì was unusually stern and severe.
His servant, Dù Liàng, served him for more than ten years.
Xiāo Yǐngshì would often beat him more than a hundred times.
Unable to bear the suffering,
some people encouraged him to choose a better master.
其僕曰：
「我非不能他從，
所以遲留者特愛慕其博奧。」
Lǐ Rǒng, *Dú Yì Zhì* His servant said, "It's not that I can't follow others, but the reason I linger is that I especially admire his erudition and depth." Lǐ Rǒng, *Record of Unique Matters*.
當千
the Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Carriages, Zhào Zòng, was the son-in-law of Guō Zǐyí.
Because the slave Dāngqiān exposed his secret affairs, he was imprisoned.
Dāngqiān was kept within the palace.
Zhāng Yì of the Palace Secretariat memorialized, saying:
"Dàzōng said to his attendants:
Recently, there have been slaves accusing their masters,

From now on, those slaves who accuse their masters

By the time the great bandits attacked the capital twenty years later,

Sù had an old estate in Nányáng.
He always ordered Hóng to collect rent,
and it always arrived on schedule.
He traveled thousands of *lǐ* back and forth without ever pocketing a single coin.
After he passed the imperial examination,

When one spring's affairs were completed,

Wǔ Gōnggàn.
Wǔ Gōnggàn served Kuǎi Xīyì for more than ten years,
being exceptionally diligent.
When Xīyì was promoted,
Gōnggàn resigned, saying his parents were alive
and he wished to return home to care for them.
The Duke tried to keep him but couldn't.
The Duke, recognizing his loyalty and filial piety,
sent him off with a poem,
which vaguely said, "Amidst dangerous mountains, I never left my horse;
after being drunk,
I often saw it standing before my bed."
Colleagues collected silk to give him as a farewell gift,
and all composed poems in response.

The entire army was wiped out.
Áng 高昂, on a light horse, fled eastward to Hēyáng Héyáng River-North city.

Reading
The male and female slaves in Zhèng Xuán's household all read books.

Dí Sù of Kuàijī,

Sù said,

disgrace the name of Sù's maid."

Married Maid
Zhào Míngfǔ, whose name was Rénměi,
was from Tianshui.
He was transferred and appointed magistrate of Pú County.
He was inherently knowledgeable of the "Three Destinies" (i.e., astrology, fate),
and knew his own destiny and lifespan.
A fortune-teller passed by and visited him,
and their predictions matched.
Zhào had a daughter who was not yet married.
He had not yet chosen a son-in-law.
In the meantime, he first sought a maidservant for his daughter.
One day, he ordered her to sweep the courtyard.
Suddenly, she burst into tears.
Zhào asked why.
The woman said:
"My surname is Wáng,
my father's name is Délín,
he once served as magistrate of this town.
I was born in this county,
but after losing my parents,
I was abducted and sold here."
Zhào, astonished, said to his wife:
"My daughter need not worry about not marrying."
He then chose a kind and wealthy resident of the town, withdrew the woman's dowry,
and married her off first.
Suddenly, one day, a skilled physiognomist passed by,
and again paid his respects to the magistrate.
Upon seeing him, he was greatly alarmed and said:
"Yesterday, when I observed your face,
your life seemed to be ending soon.
Today, when I observe it,
your blessings, prosperity, and longevity are beyond description."
He then inquired about his extraordinary policies and the clearing of unjust cases.
Zhào said:
"I have no other notable policies."
So he spoke of the matter of marrying off the servant girl.
Thereupon, he congratulated the magistrate, saying:
"This alone is unseen merit, prosperity, and longevity.
How can it be measured?"
From "Records of Searching for the Spirits".
Nowadays, various books only record the affairs of Zhōng Lí Jǐn of the Southern Tang Dynasty.

During the reign of Emperor Gāozōng 高宗, the kingdom of Zhōu Chéng 周澄 sent an envoy to submit a memorial, saying: "The Hējiā 訶伽 kingdom has a white elephant with
four tusks hanging from its head and five feet moving its body. Wherever the elephant is, the land is sure to be fertile. It possesses both power and
the ability to quell disasters. Its strength equals that of ten elephants, and it can restrain a hundred men. Washing its tusks with water and drinking it cures diseases. We request that you send
troops to welcome it and present it as tribute." The Emperor said to his attending officials: "If we establish a law of frugality, its flaw will still be extravagance; who
can control it? Therefore, the sages used a simple mat to show frugality and a thatched roof to warn against extravagance. The *Shū* (Book of Documents) says: 'Rare birds and strange
beasts should not be raised in the state,' knowing they are of no benefit, the source must not be blocked. What use do I have for this elephant, to have it sent from afar,
thus troubling its envoy and sending him back?"
*Táng Shū* (Book of Tang)
Emperor Mínghuáng 明皇 always bestowed lavish feasts, ascending the tower and leading out large elephants and rhinoceroses, which would either bow or dance, moving in time with the music.
